On the Orders of the Day:

I wish to draw the attention of the Government to an artiqje which appeared in the Financial Times of the 3rd instant, stating in effect that Premier Borden had communicated with the Dominion Iron and Steel Company and advised them that they were not to amalgamate with the Nova Scotia Steel and Coal Company, and that this action on his part had been suggested, if not insisted upon, by the British Government. I wish first to -know whether it is true that the British Government has taken the position of advising our Prime Minister what should be done in connection with Canadian local affairs; and, if true, I would ask how the Government reconciles that position with its somewhat loud protestations in this House of the growth of nationality?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
In answer to my hon. friend's
rather rhetorical question, I may suggest to him that the British Government is not at all likely to interfere, and has not to my knowledge interfered, in any way in such a matter of purely Dominion jurisdiction as the one brought to our attention. So I think I can ease his mind at once

as to that. T may say further that it is not within my knowledge that the Prime Minister has recently communicated in any way with the Dominion Iron and Steel Company or the Nova Scotia Steel Company with regard bo the' matter in question. It did receive some attention during the war, when, I believe, it was thought decidedly inadvisable that the control of the steel industry in Canada should pass from Canadian hands. So far as I am concerned, that would be my position to-day.
May I ask my hon. friend the President of the Council, if the Government has received any communication from the Amalgamated Postal Workers in reference to a possible strike?

speakeroldname: Hon. N. W. ROWELL (President of the Privy Council):
speechtext:
On May 7, the Postmaster General received the following telegram from the Secretary of the Amalgamated Postal Workers, Mr. J. A. Elrick:
Events seem to indicate re-classification will not go through Parliament this session or it it does we will not have time to represent our opinion. If so must remind you our most important questions were deferred pending same and pre'sent restlessness will immediately develop trouble when prorogation becomes obvious. Would appreciate statement for information of membership.
To which the Postmaster General replied on the 8th:
Tour fears absolutely groundless. Newspaper reports entirely without foundation. Matter being printed every day and will be taken up as soon as bound and ready. It will unquestionably be attended to this session and every opportunity given to postal workers for examination.
That apparently did not satisfy some members of the Association, and the Postmaster General received a further telegram on Sunday afternoon pressing for a statement that the re-classification would be brought down this week, to which he replied in accordance with the statement made by the Acting Minister of Trade and Commerce (Hon. A. K. Maclean) in the House yesterday. I have also received the following telegram from Mr. Elrick:
Re-classification Bill promised May first covers most important grievances of postal workers and its non-appearance and general upheaval driving members beyond control and when definite steps are taken only complete settlement will suffice. Official notification of impatient action will reach me within three days and only quick showing of re-classification

will stand the general demands for a tie up and the keystone of the trouble being Government employees will create a dangerous movement at this time. I appeal to you to have re-classification in the House not later than Tuesday.
When the representatives of the Western Postal Workers were here they interviewed the Civil Service Commission and the experts who were re-classifying the service, and they had exactly the same knowledge as the Government had as to when the reclassification would be brought down. They were informed, as the Government was, that it was anticipated that the re-classification would be ready in time to enable the Acting Minister of Trade and Commerce (Hon. A. K. Maclean) to present the Bill to the House during the first week in May. Last night, therefore, I replied as follows:-
Referring your night letter, you and your associates conferred with Civil Service Commission and experts while here and you know we had assurance from them that the re-classica-tion would be completed so that it could be presented to House during first week of May and it was relying on this that Government made its promise to you. Government has been urging utmost expedition and we feel sure that Civil Service Commission and experts have done everything in their power to get schedules completed but it has not been humanly possible to do so. As Postmaster General has wired you schedules are now completed and are all In printers' hands and Printing Bureau has been instructed to have them translated and printed as rapidly as possible. Am advised by Civil Service Commission that printing which has already commenced will take substantially longer than originally estimated and this is one explanation of delay but as everything relates back to first of April, Post Office employees cannot be prejudiced in any way by unavoidable though regrettable delay, and precipitate action on their part would be wholly unjustifiable.
It has been intimated that the post office employees may go out on a sympathetic strike with other parties striking in certain sections of Western Canada. The Government's view is that such a course would be .wholly unjustifiable. The Government has taken every possible step to bring the reclassification down at the earliest practicable date, and the post office employees will be in no wise prejudiced by a few days' delay, because the re-classification relates back to the first of April.

On motion of Sir Thomas White (Acting Prime Minister), Bill No. 68, for granting to His Majesty aid for demobilization and other purposes, was read the third time.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
That the said Bill do now pass and that the title be as on the Order Paper.
He said: I desire to say a few words on account of a discussion which took place in the Committee stage with respect to the borrowing powers which this Bill authorizes. I find upon inquiry that as it stands the Bill is satisfactory to my department. The amount which it authorizes the Government to borrow is $350,000,000, less any amount borrowed in excess of the amounts authorized by any War Appropriation Act. That means that to the extent to which we have over-borrowed in respect of past-war appropriations, the $350,000,000 will be reduced. If we have borrowed $100,000,000 in excess of the amount authorized by previous War Appropriation Acts, then the maximum amount which we could borrow under this Bill would be $250,000,000. I was under a slight misapprehension the other night when the Bill was in the Committee stage, and the point drawn to my attention by the member for Shelburne and Queens (Mr. Fielding) was well taken; that is to say, that section 4 of the Bill authorizes the borrowing of $350,000,000, but less any amounts that have been over-borrowed in respect of previous War Appropriation Acts. The result of this legislation, so far as borrowing powers are concerned, will be-with previous legislation-to give the Government power to borrow for war purposes only to the extent for which expenditures have been authorized by the Acts in question, and no more. Any further borrowing power which the Dominion Govern-

ment may require in respect of the expenditures authorized hy Parliament, either previously or at this session, will be provided for by other legislation. I think, therefore, that the Bill, as it stands, should pass.
Mr. Speaker-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: The Bill has been given its third reading, and the motion that the title pass is not debatable. I thought it was due to the Acting Prime Minister that he should make the explanation which he wished to make, and there should be no objection to the leader of the Opposition putting a question; but there can be no debate on this motion.
I did not intend to enter into any debate. I simply want to inquire how much over-borrowing is to be covered by this Bill. What is the exact borrowing power of the Bill?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

On motion of Hon. A. K. Maclean (Acting Minister of Trade and Commerce) the House went into Committee to consider the following proposed resolution:
That it is expedient to provide,-
(1)	That every can, carton, bottle, box, barrel, wrapper, package or closed receptacle containing human food or any other commodity manufactured, produced, sold or offered for sale in Canada, when such container is in its original unopened or unbroken form as it is usually delivered to consumers when sold or offered for sale in Canada, should be plainly marked, branded or stamped with the name and address of the fillers, and the weight, measure or quantity of the contents of the container;
(2)	That this proposed legislation shall not apply to packages for export from Canada, or goods sold in bulk or broken packages, or fresh fruit and vegetables, or articles held in stock by a wholesale or retail dealer prior to the coming into force of the proposed legislation, or .
TSir Thomas White.]
packages containing two avoirdupois ounces or less, or one fluid ounce or less, or to any article the sale of which as regards the weight or marking thereof is already provided for under other statutes;	V
(3)	That tolerance and variations shall be allowed for discrepancies due exclusively to errors in weighing, measuring or counting which occur in packing conducted in compliance with good commercial practice, or due exclusively to differences in atmospheric conditions, evaporation or absorption of water;

iMr. ROBB: When similar legislation was before the House last year, objection was 'taken that it would impose additional obligations upon farmers who fill milk and cream for shipment to the cities, and that it would add considerably to the price paid by the consumer. Has the minister taken that into consideration? I presume he has looked up the debate upon the Bill of last year.	[DOT]

The Bill founded upon this resolution will be almost exactly the same as passed the House last year. The Bill last year was defeated in the Senate for some reason which I forget at the moment; I think it contained some provisions with regard to firewood and cement, which were objected to iby the Senate, and the Bill was not proceeded with further on that account. The Bill does not contain those provisions this year, but simply provides for the marking of containers or receptacles containing human food with the name of the manufacturer and the net weight or quantity of the contents.

Does it apply to
drugs ?

No, but I think the Act which the Bill founded on this resolution will amend applies to drugs. The draft Bill sets forth the exceptions as follows:	All goods sold in bulk or broken
packages; fresh fruits or vegetables; articles held in stock by a wholesale or retail dealer prior to the coming into force of this Act; packages containing two avoirdupois ounces or less, which packages will be exempt from marking in terms of weight; packages containing one fluid ounce or less; and any article the sale of which as regards the weight or marking thereof is already provided for under other statutes. I am not able to say at the moment whether containers containing milk, which is marketed, without being in any sense manufactured, will be exempt under this Act, and on mov-

ing the second reading I shall be in a position to answer my hon. friend.

As the resolution stands the Bill would provide that every bottle containing human food-that might be milk or cream-shall be branded or stamped with the name and address of the fillers, and the weight, measure or quantity of the contents of the container. A very large business is done to-day putting up milk in small bottles to ship them to the cities, and if the minister insists upon the legislation going through in its present form the consumer in the city will have to bear the expense of this additional work.

The enacting
clause reads as follows:
Every can, carton, bottle, box, barrel, wrapper, package or closed receptacl-e containing human food or any other commodity manufactured, produced, sold or offered for sale in Canada, when such container is in its original unopened or unbroken form as it is usually delivered to consumers when sold or offered for sale in Canada, should be plainly marked, branded or stamped with the name and address of the fillers, and the weight, measure or quantity of the contents of the container;
And so on. I am doubtful if milk would come within the meaning of the Act.
Mr. ROBB * Oh yes, it is human food.
There is no question about its being human food.
Why should not a bottle of milk be marked? Every dealer should be anxious to have his name labelled on his bottle, so as to let the public know that he is selling good stuff.
It would mean an additional expense.

Milk bottles are washed every day, or should be, and the label would be washed off.
Sir S'AM HUGHES: It would not cost a thousandth part of a cent.

I have some knowledge of the milk business, although I am not in it myself. The investment in glass bottles by the large dairy companies in the cities is very substantial, and if the legislation goes through in the form foreshadowed by the resolution I hope that ample opportunity will be given to the milk dealers to replace their bottles gradually with bottles having their names marked or blown in the glass. The suggestion of the hon. and gallant member for Victoria (Sir Sam Hughes) that the label might be pasted on
the bottle or receptacle would lead me to suppose that he thinks the bottles are washed one by one under the tap; that is not the way it is done. The bottles are washed by machinery, and the only efficacious method of marking would be to blow the name in the bottle itself. I trust that the milk dealers will be given an opportunity to use up all their old bottles before being forced to provide these new ones.

I did not suggest a mark on the bottom or on the top or anything of that kind. The label should be placed on the side of the bottle, and for the life of me I cannot see why it should not be required. Sometimes the gentleman who drinks milk will order a bottle and get good stuff, and at other times he gets only skimmed milk. The consumer after all has some rights, and one of those rights is to know whether the bottle of milk placed before him is put up by a man who puts up good milk or by a man who sails as close to the law as possible.

On motion of Sir Thomas White (Acting Prime Minister) the House went into Committee to consider the following proposed resolution, Mr. Boivin in the Chair:
Resolved, That it is expedient to bring in a measure,-
1.	To ratify and confirm the Order in Council of the twenty-fourth day of February, 1919, prohibiting the importation, manufacture and transportation of intoxicating liquors, published in an extra issue of the Canada Gazette of Monday, February 24, 1919, subject to the following amendments:-
(a)	Paragraph (c) of regulation one to he amended by striking out all the words after the word " wine " in the last line thereof and inserting in lieu thereof the words "or other intoxicating liquors of limited alcoholic content are permitted," so that the said paragraph shall read as follows :
"(c) 'Prohibited area" means any province, territory, municipality, district, county or other area wherein the sale of intoxicating liquor is under or by any law, Federal or Provincial, prohibited, and shall include any such area wherein the sale of native wine or other intoxicating liquors of limited alcoholic content are permitted."

(c)	Subsection three of said regulation three to be amended by striking out the words " until the thirtieth day of April, 1919," at the end thereof, and substituting therefor the words ** or to sending, taking, transporting or delivering any intoxicating liquor lawfully manufactured in any province to any place in such province where such intoxicating liquor may lawfully be sold," so that the said subsection shall read as follows:

" (4) No person after the first day of April, 1918, shall either directly or indirectly sell or contract or agree to sell any intoxicating liquor which is to be delivered within any area where the sale of such intoxicating liquor is forbidden."
2.	To ratify and confirm the Order in Council of the twelfth day of April, 1919, concerning the disposal of intoxicating liquors forfeited to the Crown, published in the Canada Gazette of Saturday, the nineteenth day of April, 1919.
3.	To provide that for the purposes of this proposed legislation and the schedule thereto comprising the said Orders in Council, the sale of any intoxicating liquor shall be deemed to be forbidden or prohibited in any province, territory, municipality, district, county or other area where the sale of the same is forbidden, except for use in divine service, for medical purposes, for manufacturing or commercial purposes, other than for the manufacture or use thereof as a beverage, or for other similar purposes.
4.	To provide that the Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue shall have power to make such regulations as he may deem necessary to prevent intoxicating liquor from being illegally manufactured in or from being imported into

Canada, or from being sold, sent, taken, transported or delivered in violation of this proposed legislation and the schedule thereto comprising the said Orders in Council. Any person violating the provisions of any such regulation or of the proposed legislation shall be liable to the penalty prescribed for violation of the provisions of the regulation contained in the said Orders in Council.-The Prime Minister.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
As this is important legislation I think the Committee will expect a statement with respect to its purpose and scope. The object of the legislation which this resolution has in view is to ratify and confirm certain Orders in Council which were passed by the Government during the war under the authority of the War Measures Act, for the purpose of restricting, during the continuance of the war and for a period of twelve months thereafter, the manufacture, transportation and importation of intoxicating liquors as defined by the Orders in Council. The definition of "intoxicating liquors" is to be found in the consolidated order which was dated February 24, 1919, and which is as follows:
Intoxicating liquor means and includes any liquor or beverage which contains more than 2J per centum of proof spirit.
Dealing with the various res trictions, I may point out that by the provisions of the consolidated Order in Council, no intoxicating liquor was to be imported into Canada after December 24, 1917, unless actually purchased for importation before that date, and actually shipped before January 31, 1918. Provision was also made in that connection that satisfactory evidence of such shipment had to be submitted to the Minister of Customs. The prohibition against importation was not to apply to wine for use in divine service, to intoxicating liquor used for medicinal purposes, to intoxicating liquor used for manufacturing purposes, and in this latter case provision was made for a special license to be issued by the Minister of Inland Revenue for such manufacture.
The effect of the Order in Council was to prohibit the manufacture of intoxicating liquors after April 1, 1918. There was in that connection a proviso that in case the sale for beverage purposes of any intoxicating liquor was permitted in a province such liquor might be manufactured until December 31, 1918. Manufacture was permitted under license in the case of liquors to be used for sacramental, industrial, artistic, mechanical, scientific or medicinal purposes. In regard to the third restriction, namely, upon the transportation of

intoxicating liquors, this was forbidden into any prohibited area in Canada after April 1, 1918. "Prohibited area" is defined by the consolidated Order in Council to mean
Any province, territory, municipality, district, county or other area wherein the sale of intoxicating liquor is in or by any law, federal or provincial, prohibited and shall include any such area wherein the sale of native wine is prohibited.
In connection with the restriction upon transportation, provision was made to meet the case of shipments actually made before April 1, 1918, delivery to be not later than the date at which such liquor would be delivered in the ordinary course, and in any case not later than May 1, 1918. There was a further provision that no contract should be made to sell after April 1, 1918, although a licensee might send into any prohibited area for delivery for authorized purposes intoxicating liquors in accordance with the terms of the license issued to him by the Minister of Inland Revenue. Similar licensees in prohibited areas' were authorized to receive intoxicating liquors under the terms of their license and not otherwise. There was a further regulation made to ensure that such transportation should be only by common carriers, by rail or water, to the end that the provision of the Order in Council might be more effectively carried out.
The purposes for which the Orders in Council were passed are set out in the recital of the consolidated Order in Council as follows:
(1)	To prevent waste;
(2)	To promote thrift;
(3)	To conserve resources; and increase national efficiency.
As I stated, the duration of the measure was limited by the Order in Council to the period of the war and twelve months thereafter. As the orders were passed^ under the authority of the War Measures'Act, it is necessary that they should be now ratified and confirmed by Parliament if they are to continue in effect as was the intention for a period of twelve months after the conclusion of the war.

Does the twelve
months mean from the signing of the armistice, or from the signing of peace?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
From the time
the conclusion of the war is officially declared. The present position is that we are still at war with Germany, Austro-Hungary, Turkey and Bulgaria. There seems to be no doubt that the period which the Order in
Council was intended to cover was the remaining period of the war until officially at an end and twelve months thereafter. The consolidated Order in Council points out that the regulations made therein are to be construed as supplementary to the prohibitory laws now in force, or that may hereafter be in force, in a province or territory and that such regulations should continue in force during, as I have stated, the period of the present war and twelve months thereafter.
It was felt by the Government that the period succeeding the war would, as to many of its characteristics, be similar to the war period. Further, it would be the time of demobilization and it was believed that the country would, for at least a year after the war, be subject to what would virtually be war expenditure and that is' the case to-day. The Order in Council therefore provided that the legislation enacted, for it was legislation under the authority, as I have said, of the War Measures Act, should continue during the war and for a period of twelve months thereafter when it was expected that demobilization would be completed.
The resolution provides for certain amendments to the consolidated Order in Council and the other orders w'hich were passed for the purpose of more effectually carrying out the provisions of the consolidated order. "Intoxicating liquors," was defined by the consolidated order to mean and include liquor exceeding a strength of two and a half per cent of proof spirit. At the time the order was passed there was prohibitory legislation, I think, in all the provinces under which the two and a half per cent of proof spirit standard had been adopted. Since the armistice, and as a result of a plebiscite in the province of Quebec, it is lawful under the laws of that province to sell for beverage purposes liquor to the strength of five per cent of proof spirit and, in the special case of wine, 6.98 per cent alcohol.
In the province of Ontario announcement has been made that a plebiscite or referendum will be taken, and it may be that other provinces will pursue a similar course. The Government, therefore, thought it advisable-in view of what has taken place in Quebec and Ontario, and what may take place in other provinces-to modify the Order in Council to the extent, and to the extent only, necessary to permit effect to be given to provincial laws respecting the sale of liquor for beverage purposes. We have therefore provided, as an amendment to the consolidated Order in Council, that liquor may be manufactured within

a province to the standard of strength authorized by the laws of that province for sale for beverage purposes. To use a concrete illustration:	It will be permissible when
this resolution is carried into law for brewers in the province of Quebec to manufacture beer to the strength of five per cent proof spirits in order that it may be available for sale and consumption as authorized by the laws of that province.
Would the minister kindly explain what " proof spirits " means? Those of us who are strictly temperate men, like the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Rowell), do not know the meaning of the term.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am so strong a temperance man myself that I could not really give my hon. friend what would be regarded as a scientific definition, but it might be right to say-
Perhaps the President of the Privy Council can give us a definition?	[DOT]

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: -that alcohol has about twice the strength of proof spirits- or in other words, that two and a half per cent of alcohol is about the equivalent of five per cent of proof spirits. It is said, and some hon. gentlemen will be able to pronounce as to this very much better than myself, that there is not as much " bite " in the proof spirit beverage, as there is in the alcohol beverage of the same apparent percentage. I think I have stated to the House in sufficient detail the legal effect of the Order in Council and of the modification which we now propose. I have caused to be laid upon the Table a number of copies-sufficient I think for the use of members-of the consolidated Order in Council and the two amendments referred to.
The Acting Prime Minister has given some explanation regarding the use of beer. Would he supplement that explanation by further details in connection, for instance, with the use of wine.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: As to what?
As to the sort of wine which is to be permitted to be consumed in the province of Quebec?
Or in any other province?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
That is a matter which we had under consideration. I understand that Quebec does not manufacture

nativS wine to any great extent. Am I right in that understanding?
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The question then arises as to how native wine, or at least wine of the strength authorized there by provincial laws, will be provided to meet the requirements of the people for beverage purposes. I may say to my hon. friend that it was my intention to have modified this Order in Council to the extent necessary by providing that there might be imported into the province of Quebec, or into any other province where similar legislation might prevail, wine of the strength permitted by such legislation. I was informed, possibly erroneously, that there are no wines likely to come from France of as low an alcoholic standard as the wine which is authorized for sale now by the legislation of the province of Quebec to which I have referred;.but in order to carry out the principle which I have indicated, I should be prepared to consider an amendment to the resolution which would provide for the importation into a province of wine not exceeding the alcoholic standard authorized by the law of that province. Such an amendment might provide for importation from a country outside of Canada, or for transportation from another province in Canada, into any province where such a law as I have mentioned is in effect. If any hon. member is in a position to say whether wine is likely to be imported, especially from France, of the alcoholic strength which is now lawful by the laws of the province of Quebec in liquor for beverage purposes, I shall be glad to hear his representations in that regard.
I do not know but that the Acting Prime Minister could have made himself more clear if he had a little of the beverage which he has been describing.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Two and-a-half
per cent?

It would have steadied his nerve; he is a little nervous in his explanations. I do not know whether the President of the Privy Council would not have given the explanation much better. I cannot see why this burning and shining light of temperance is over-shadowed by the Acting Prime Minister to-day; we thought this was the former's special sphere. But what I wanted to ask is, why not
4 p.m. make this general rule applicable to all provinces? Why should the maker of wine in Ontario be prohibited

from selling his product in, Quebec, provided he is not violating the laws of that province, and so on? Make it a universal rule. If France wants us to import strong wines and the province of Quebec will not allow it, there is no harm done; but if that province wishes to import strong wines from France and the laws of Quebec permit it, why not allow such importation?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I have already stated that I would be prepared to consider an amendment, after discussion in the House, which would permit wine to be imported from France, or any other country, and from any province in Canada, such as Ontario, where native wine is manufactured, into a province whose laws authorize its sale for beverage purposes.
What will be the effect of the law as it will stand in respect to wines in. Ontario where they are manufactured?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Under the law as it will stand?
What will happen to the wines of Ontario, what will be the effect of the law as to them?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The position is that native wine in the province of Ontario may continue to be manufactured because by the legislation of that province there is no restriction upon its sale-that is an exception.
(Regardless of percentage of alcohol?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is permitted today by the laws of the province of Ontario.
What strength?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There is no limit as to strength.
As I understand the resolution, it would prohibit the importation into the province of Quebec of beer manufactured in the province of Ontario?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Y"es.
That seems to me to create a monopoly in the province of Quebec, and all monopolies are obnoxious and vicious.
We will have to drink the whole of it; we cannot export it.

You will have to drink the whole of it at a price fixed by your manufacturer. I have not considered the matter sufficiently to give an opinion, but if my recollection of the British North America
Act is correct, it seems to me there is difficulty in the way of legislation of this sort. Section 121 of the Act says that the growth, produce, or manufacture of a province shall be admitted free into another province. That, of course, does relate to duty in the sense of customs duty, but it must necessarily mean free importation. How can this Parliament create a monopoly so that one province alone shall have the right to manufacture and sell within its boundaries an article which may be manufactured in another province? I do not know whether the Government has considered that question, but it seems to me there is some difficulty in the way, apart altogether from the point I raise as to a monopoly being created. There are probably millions of dollars invested in breweries in the province of Ontario. Why should not the brewers of that province have the right of entry into the province of Quebec in competition with Quebec brewers, when the latter province gives to its people the right to purchase beer of a certain quality?
We have no objection.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The constitutional question raised by the hon. gentleman was considered carefully by the Department of Justice, and they reached the conclusion that the Government was within its powers in enacting the Order in Council as it stands.

Is it quite clear and beyond dispute that in the province of Ontario, which I understood was a prohibition province, one has the right to get drunk, provided he gets drunk on native wine? Is that the law?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not think it is so specified in the law. ,

For the information of the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding) I might say that the Ontario law does not allow the retail sale of wine other than in undisturbed packages to the house of a consumer; it does not allow the sale of wine over the bar.

The hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's has raised a question on what has always appeared to me to be the most extraordinary piece of legislation perpetrated by the province of Ontario. There is no doubt that that province has enacted what is in effect the clearest kind of class legislation. It allows, as the hon. member for Lincoln (Mr. Chaplin) has just stated, the sale of wine, the strength of which is not specified. This is

the clause of the Ontario Act covering this point:
Subject to any regulations or restrictions which the Board may impose, manufacturers of native wines, from grapes grown and produced in Ontario, may sell the same in wholesale quantities only, that is to say in quantities of not less than five gallons in each cask or vessel at any one time and when sold in bottles not less than one dozen bottles of at least three half pints at any one time.
Now, the law of the province of Ontario, as I understand it, did not prohibit-I am subject to correction as to this-the manufacture of ale of any strength for export, and if the breweries of Ontario found a market in foreign countries they were entitled to manufacture and export. Under the proposed resolution and Order in Council that market is cut off. Not only are they prohibited from exporting to the province of Quebec beer of 5 per cent proof spirits, or 21 per cent alcohol, whatever the ruling in Quebec may he-but they cannot export to any other country. That seems to me such an absurd and illogical position that I propose an amendment to the resolution. Subsection 3 of paragraph (c) of the resolution reads as follows:
(3) No person after the first day of April, 1918, shall send, take, transport into, or deliver in any prohibited area any intoxicating liquor, or cause any intoxicating liquor to be sent, transported or delivered. Provided that any intoxicating liquor actually shipped before the first day of April, 1918, may be delivered in such prohibited area by a common carrier within such period of time as is required for such delivery under the ordinary and usual conditions governing the business of such common carrier but not later than the first day of May, A.D., 1918. Provided that this regulation shall not apply to the sending, taking, transporting or delivering of native wines in the province of Ontario, or to sending, taking, transporting or delivering any intoxicating liquor lawfully manufactured in any province to any place in such province where such intoxicating liquor may lawfully be sold.
By amendment I propose to strike out these words:
Sending, taking, transporting or delivering of native wines in the province of Ontario.
If we are to have this legislation imposed let us have it imposed fairly. Do not let us make an exception in the case of some one favoured class or province. I beg therefore, Mr. Chairman, to move that amendment.
iSir THOMAS WHITE:	It is a complicated piece of legislation and I would ask the hon. member if he will kindly give notice of his resolution.

Might I make a
suggestion to the Acting Prime Minister in
LMr. Cronyn.J
that very regard? Why not have the Order in Council printed so that we can deal with the matter intelligently? I do not suppose it is a very voluminous affair; it will only take a day.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Copies of the
Order in Council are laid upon the Table for the use of hon. members. I think the resolution shows clearly the effect of the amendments which we propose. I still do not quite appreciate the point made by my hon. friend from London (Mr. Cronyn) and I would be glad if he would state again what he has in mind in the amendment.

By this legislation we
are backing up the exceedingly unfair legislation of the province of Ontario. And we are going further; we are adopting, as I understand the resolution, the sale of liquor in the province as a test. As I said, under the legislation of the province of Ontario brewers and wine merchants alike were permitted to manufacture for export, I speak subject to correction.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not understand that the legislation of the province of Ontario prevents the manufacture of wine and beer for export. The jurisdiction of a province is with respect of the sale and consumption; the question of manufacture and export I think is a Dominion matter.

That is undoubtedly
right, Mr. Chairman. But the province recognized that situation by providing as follows in section 45 of the Ontario Temperance Act:
Nothing herein contained- shall prevent any brewer, distiller or other person duly licensed by the Government of Canada for the manufacture of spirituous, fermented or other liquor, from keeping or having liquor manufactured by him in any building where such manufacture is carried on.
The provincial authorities knew that they had not the right to prohibit the manufacture, and under the law as it stands the wine merchant and the brewer can and do manufacture for export. Under this Order in Council manufacture for export must cease, and that being the case we should be logical. If we are going to be temperate, let us be temperate. Why should the manufacture and sale in Ontario of wine which runs from sixteen to twenty per cent proof spirits be permitted, while the manufacture and sale of beer of five per cent is not permitted?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The principle
which should underly the action of the Dominion with respect to legislation of this

kind is recognition of the rights of the provinces to enact such legislation, within their jurisdiction as they may deem proper. It is true that the legislation of Ontario excepted native wines. No doubt they did so upon considerations which appeared proper to them as representatives of the people of Ontario. The hon. member sees an unfairness in permitting the manufacture of wine of unlimited strength in Ontario, while at the same time a limitation as to strength is imposed in respect of beer manufactured in the province. But that is essentially a matter for the legislature of Ontario. If Ontario, acting within its jurisdiction, sees fit to enact that beer for beverage purposes shall not be sold in Ontario of greater strength than two and a half per cent of proof spirits and at the same time feels justified in authorizing the manufacture and sale of native wine in the province, I suppose that is a matter for the legislature and the people of Ontario. I do not know how far we should be justified in reviewing their action with respect to what is clearly within their jurisdiction under the British North America Act. I am of the opinion that this Order in Council does not prohibit the export of native wine manufactured in Ontario. If Ontario adopted legislation under which -pine of a strength not exceeding, let us say, five per cent alcohol, should be sold for beverage purposes there, then under this legislation they could not, I think, manufacture beyond that strength, either for domestic use or for export. But Ontario, I understand, has not placed any limitation upon the strength of native wine manufactured there.

Would the minister be averse to an amendment permitting Ontario to export to Quebec its native wines at the strength which Quebec allows? Moreover, does this resolution stop the exportation of beer from Ontario to points outside that province?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
According to the law of Quebec, wine of the alcoholic strength of a little under seven per cent is authorized for sale for beverage purposes. Unless that legislation is to be defeated by Dominion enactment, it is necessary to permit importation into Quebec from outside of Canada or transportation into Quebec from any other province where such wine is manufactured. I have stated that I would be prepared to consider a suggestion for permitting the importation from outside of Canada into a province
such as Quebec of wine of the strength authorized for sale for beverage purposes by the legislation of that province; and also the transportation into such province from another province where wine is manufactured for the purpose of supplying local requirements in strict accordance with the laws of that province. With regard to beer, the situation is somewhat different. Beer may 'be manufactured in any province to the extent of the quantity required to meet the consumption needs in accordance with the provincial laws. I think the same statement might be made with regard to whisky. With regard to wine, it is only in some provinces that native wine is manufactured. But if any difficulty arises with regard to the logic of the situation I suppose we would have to meet the condition in a province such as Quebec by permitting importation from outside. There seems to be a very strong sentiment in the community that if a province by its legislation prohibits the sale for beverage purposes within that province of liquor beyond a certain strength, the manufacture of liquor beyond that strength in that province should not be permitted.

Instead of labelling one law for one province and another for another, why not make our legislation universal and apply the same form of legislation to all provinces-having regard, of course, to existing provincial laws?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend will not find the name of any province mentioned in this resolution, or in any amendment. The amendments to the resolution are for the purpose of enabling effect to be given to provincial legislation in any province. I used the illustration of Quebec because Quebec has taken action and no other province up to date has.

Suppose Ontario refuses to go beyond the two-and-a-half per cent for beer, and Quebec goes five; would it be impossible for a brewer in Ontario to make his beer up to five per cent for sale in the province of Quebec?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It would under this resolution.

I should like, in the first place, to straighten out the hon. member for Victoria (Sir Sam Hughes) as to the meaning of "proof spirits," and I am surprised that the hon. member, so rich in military lore, is not familiar with the historic association between proof spirits

and military regulations. The term had its origin in England in the old days when the army was armed with flintlock rifles. In those days it took a certain percentage of alcohol to get the powder to the point where it would explode with a spark. It was found through experiments made by the British army that alcohol could be considerably reduced in (strength and still strike fire when used in the flintlock rifle. When the alcohol was reduced to the lowest point at which it would strike fire, it was known as "proof spirits;" it was the test or the "proof." While alcohol has a strength of 165, they could reduce it to a strength of 100, and at that strength the powder would strike fire. That was the origin of the term or standard known as "proof strength."
I want to say a word on the principle involved in the resolution now before the House, because, if I understand parliamentary procedure, we are in order in dis-culssing the principle of the legislation at this stage, and the details later. The Acting Prime Minister has emphasized more than once to-day that this legislation is to give effect so far as possible to the intention and the desire of the provinces as expressed by the legislation enacted by the different provinces. That, I submit, is precisely what will not be done by the legislation founded on this resolution. True, the resolution has been drawn in such a way as carefully to safeguard the wishes and intentions of the province of Quebec, but I submit that it shows no desire or any intention to meet the views of the legislature of the province of Ontario. The connection in which I raise the question of the Legislature of Ontario is this: This legislation is intended to prevent the importation into the province of Ontario of alcoholic liquors of a strength in excess of two-and-a-half per cent proof spirits. Now I submit that in the province of Ontario there has been no desire or attempt on the part of the legislature to avail itself of the rights which it had under the existing law prior to the Order in Council of March of last year, to put an embargo on the importation of alcoholic beverages into the province. I submit that the province of Ontario at the present time has the right to do everything which this legislation proposes to do with reference to importation into the province. The legislature of the province of Ontario has an absolutely legal right under the Doherty Act of 1916, passed by this House, to do exactly what is here attempted to be done in a paternal way. For that reason, I submit that if there is a

desire on the part of this Government to give effect to the rights of the provinces to deal as fully as lies within their power with the question of prohibition, then, to be consistent, the whole question should be left to the Government of Ontario to be dealt with by them. I believe that it is the opinion of the province of Ontario that the provincial Government at Toronto was dealing with the question prior to the Order in Council, and is dealing with it now, in a way that is likely to give ultimately the very best results.
Just a word with reference to the Doherty Act. The question of prohibition has developed in parliamentary procedure to an extent never known before, the passing of the buck-of course, I quite understand that many honourable gentlemen do not understand the term. In 1916 when the Ontario Temperance Act was before the Ontario Legislature, the question was raised that under the British North America Act the provincial government had no right to put an embargo on the importation of spirits into the province, any more than it has a right to deal with the question of manufacture. Those of you who were in this House at that time will no doubt remember that a determined campaign was carried on for the Dominion Government to do what it was beyond the power of the province to do. The Ontario Government was quite willing to pass up to the Dominion Government the responsibility of providing the necessary legislation to prevent the importation of spirits into the province; I am dealing only with the province of Ontario because I know nothing about the conditions in the other provinces. The Dominion Government accepted that responsibility, and the Doherty Act was before this House at the same time the Ontario Temperance Act was before the Ontario House. Instead of dealing with the question definitely, the Dominion Government passed the Doherty Act, and then passed the question back to the province of Ontario saying, "Under this Act you have the necessary legislation to give effect to any law that you may pass against the importation of liquor." During the debate in this House the Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty) in reply to a question of Mr. Sinclair said (Hansard, page 2482-3):
If the hon. gentleman thinks otherwise, he entirely misapprehends the Bill. Anywhere in Canada, it will he an offence for a man to send liquor into a province where there is a law against it.	*
In introducing his legislation the Minister of Justice said that its whole object was

to give the very fullest power and authority to the Governments of the different provinces to give effect to their wishes in respect of matters which, under the British North America Act, they might otherwise be prevented from dealing with. I am not arguing the question one way or the other but what I say is this: In this respect the legislation before us does not give to the province of Ontario that same measure of provincial control over this question that it is so solicitous to give to the province of Quebec. If, in the opinion of the province of Ontario, there should be an embargo on the importation of spirits into the province, I say that without reference to this Order in Council at all, the province had and has a right to prevent the importation. It might very well be said that this was not law when the Ontario Temperance Act was passed. If that means that this Act had not been passed in this House at the time the Ontario Temperance Act was finally passed in Ontario, that is true. But the fact is that the resolution was in the House and the Bill had been introduced. Apart from that, however, the Ontario Legislature met in 1917, prior to the Order in Council, and there was no suggestion by either the Government of Ontario or the Opposition of Ontario asking for the legislation that is now enacted by this Order in Council. I desire to deal with another feature oi this Order in Council, and a feature of the law that will be enacted in pursuance of the resolution. When the Order in Council was passed last year, as all hon. members will remember, it did not become effective until a future date fixed in the Order. It was passed early in March and became effective on the first of April. It would have been just as easy under the provisions of the War Measures Act and under the Order in Council to have had it effective at once. And I submit that there can be only one inference, namely, that the period between the time the Order in Council was passed and the date upon which it became effective was left in order that the people affected might be permitted to stock up, and they did stock up. If it was wrong for a man to have liquor in his possession, there could be no hardship in making the Order in Council effective at once, thereby placing all citizens on the same basis. The result of its not being made effective immediately was that in Ontario those who had the inclination, the foresight and the money- particularly the money-stocked for their requirements for a very long period in the future. There is no possible question about that, and we are face to face 150
with this fact to-day-and I want to impress upon the Government that this is a view of the question which no Government can afford to overlook-that there cannot possibly be a more dangerous form of class legislation than is contained in the legislation which it is now proposed to enact in this House. We virtually say to the people of this country: If you have had the inclination and the means to stock your cellar and to provide against all your requirements for any length of 'time in the future, the law will protect you. But if, on the other hand, you have not done this, if you have been abroad during the past four years and have not had the opportunity to provide yourselves with alcoholic beverages, there is no way by which you can get them under the law. I submit that if there is going to be an absolute embargo on the importation of alcoholic beverages the Government should have the courage of its convictions and should make it illegal to have private stocks except for medicinal purposes and under the order of a physician. That would place all people on the same basis. Those who represent cities will bear me out when I say that it is fast becoming an established fact in the larger centres that there is no recognized property in whisky. In the city of Toronto, those who are in a position to know, will tell you, Mr. Chairman, that there are on an average as many as twenty and twenty-five cases- of theft from private places in a day, where houses are broken into and nothing of value removed except whisky. We do not hear much about that, because the long suffering people of Toronto would sooner lose their whisky in silence than have any one know that they had it. I clipped from a paper to-day the report of a case that will show what a grave injustice will exist in this connection. It is from Ontario and I shall not mention the name. The report says:
The ihome of Brig.-Gen	was entered
by burglars last evening and eleven cases of liquor were stolen from the wine cellar. The oases were carried to a wooded part of the grounds, where the contents were removed and taken away in an auto. There was no person
in the house at the time, Brig.-Gen	
being overseas and Mrs	in Atlantic
City.
Thousands, and hundreds of thousands, of men are coming home, and I think it would be a mistake on the part of this House to waive aside the importance of the feeling that is going to be created in this country if the man who has not had the opportunity or the means to " stock up "



realizes that his next door neighbour has a well stocked cellar,
Could they not visit their neighbours?

They do sometimes when they are away. I submit that it is within the power of this Government to enact that there shall not be any private stocks. If the Government does not do that ftien I think the matter should be left to be dealt with by the province, and under the Doherty Act it is absolutely clear that they have the legal right to deal with it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Just to advert
to two or three points made by my hon. friend in his very interesting speech. I do not understand that he is suggesting that this Government is asking Parliament to " pass the buck "-to use a vernacular expression that has never appealed to me. We are asking Parliament to pass this resolution. Let me put myself right with the House in view of the implication of the hon. gentleman that nearly all the houses in the city of Toronto, in which I have the honour to live, are largely stocked with intoxicating liquors. I can assure my hon. friend that if he visited my house he would find it very much in the condition of Mother Hubbard's cupboard, and I think that that is the case with regard to the vast majority of houses in Toronto, as in other cities in the province of Ontario. My hon. friend says that under the Canada Temperance Act, while there was a prohibition against the sale, for beverage purposes, or liquor beyond a certain alcoholic strength, it was open to the citizens of the province of Ontario to buy intoxicating liquors from adjacent provinces and have them sent directly to them for their use. He argues that if a province desired to prevent that state of affairs it had the power to do so, and I think from a strictly legal standpoint he is correct in that statement. I think the province of Ontario, through its legislature, has the power to prevent the holding of stocks of liquors for consumption by private individuals, hut my hon. friend will not fail to appreciate the impracticability of the Government of Ontario giving effect to any such legislation, which would involve a search of every house in the province, leading to a most undesirable condition of affairs.

Has the province
of Ontario the right to search?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think it has.
I do not think so.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My hon. friend
may be right, but I have the impression that the Minister of Justice stated, when the Doherty Act was before Parliament, that it was within the power of the province of Ontario, if it thought fit, to enact such legislation as would effectually prevent the bringing in of liquor from other provinces and the keeping of such liquor in the custody of citizens of Ontario.
I point out that, while that may be legally so, there are very grave practical difficulties in giving effect to such legislation. My hon. friend further argued that the province of Ontario did not ask for this legislation and that therefore it should not have been adopted by the Dominion Government. I have already pointed out that it was adopted as a war measure under the authority of the War Measures Act. The Government of Ontario was not opposed to this legislation. Let me read a telegram from the Premier of Ontario, dated December, 1917, and addressed to Sir Robert Borden, Prime Minister:
Please accept my warmest congratulations on the important action taken by your Government in connection with the liquor traffic. I am sure it will materially assist in conserving the strength of the nation for the struggle in which we are engaged.
This telegram is signed by Sir William Hearst. I put that forward to show that the province of Ontario, through its Premier, had nothing but commendation for the action taken by the Government. I think it is to be conclusively inferred from that telegram that the premier of Ontario welcomed action on the part of the Dominion Government which would prevent the importation for sale purposes into the province of Ontario of intoxicating liquors from adjacent provinces.
I submit there is a good deal to be said for that view. Let us just look at this. A province, such as Ontario, says:	There
must not be sold within this province liquor of a strength beyond two and a half per cent of proof spirits. That is what they say in the Ontario Temperance Act with respect to all liquors except native wine. If that is the deliberate judgment of the legislature, and presumably of the majority of the people of Ontario, it does seem to me that those who passed that legislation could hardly have had in contemplation a situation in which it would be largely nullified-that is if they meant it, seriously- by a round-about arrangement whereby liquor of any degree of alcoholic strength could be brought in by any citizen from an adjacent province. Some extraordinary ex-

pedients were devised. For example, a wholesaler or retailer of the province of Quebec would establish an agency in the city of Toronto, and the order would be given to the agent. The agent would then pass the order on to Quebec, the Quebec House would fill it and send the liquor back into Ontario. I need not dwell upon the incongruity of that. If the people of Ontario did not want-and do not want- liquor of a greater strength than two and a half per cent proof spirits to be consumed in Ontario, they have the right to say so. They do say it through their legislature in the law which they have enacted. I think it is clearly to be inferred from the legislation that it was not the intention of the legislature, or the Government, of Ontario, to approve the use for consumption of liquor beyond that strength. Certainly, the situation which resulted, and which I have xeferred to, did not seem to me to be a very satisfactory one. The Dominion Government, in order to implement what seemed to be the intention of the Ontario Legislature, provided that there should not be transported into the province of Ontario-I am using Ontario merely by way of illustration-from any other province liquor beyond the strength authorized for sale as a beverage by the legislature of the province. That is all we did. We decided that that should not be done for the period of the war and for twelve months after. That is the enactment that is now before this House for ratification and confirmation if Parliament should think it advisable.
The next point made by my hon. friend is that there was a period between the passing of the Act and bringing it into effect in which large quantities of intoxicating liquor were transported from one province to another, or sold within the province in which they were held, and, as he states, to enable people to " stock up." That statement is not correct. The Government had no such motive or purpose in view. The object of the provision was to enable people who had large stocks on hand for sale to partially dispose of their stocks. That is not an unusual position in connection with legislation of this kind. The effect- of this enactment, or Order in Council, was to safeguard the very serious situation, indeed, of firms who were carrying stocks of liquor which they had on hand for sale in the usual course and against which some had borrowed heavily. If suddenly without notice, or time for the partial disposal of those stocks, the Order in Council had gone into effect, and especially if permanent
150}
legislation were also passed, these people would find themselves in the position of having been financially ruined without any notice. Those were -the considerations which influenced the Government in coming to the conclusion it did.
One other point made by my hon. friend, one which is often put forward and one which is very forcible in the way in which he puts it. It is that those who had means were able to stock up and that they had their cellars full of liquor. From the way my hon. friend put it, it would appear that that was a highly desirable state of affairs from their standpoint. I do not know that it is a great advantage to a man to have his cellar full of liquor.
It seems to be so in Toronto.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Then I say it is not good for the man who has it. It is not good for any man to have too much liquor on his premises and I am a moderate in regard to that. My hon. friend puts forward the view that the public are greatly concerned about that on the theory that they have not been able to likewise stock up. I submit that that begs the whole question in so far as the provincial legislature is concerned. If the provincial legislature enacts a law, presumably, it embodies the views, opinion, wishes and desires of the people whom it represents. If the province of Ontario, through its legislature, deliberately passes an Act which contemplates that liquor beyond a -strength of two and a half proof spirits shall not be drunk in that province, in so far as they have power to prevent it, I submit that the legislature must be deemed to reflect the wishes of the majority-and the great majority-of the people of Ontario. If they do not want that situation then they can change the law. As far as Parliament is concerned, or any authority external to the province of Ontario, it seems to me that it must be conclusively assumed that the legislature of the province of Ontario speaks in its legislation for the majority of the people of the province until that legislation is changed.
I submit that that legislation does implement the legislation in force in the various provinces of Canada. The Orders in Council in question were adopted for that pur-, pose, and as a desirable war measure; to prevent waste, promote thrift and conserve resources. This is still a war year, having regard to all those purposes, and all that we are asking Parliament to do is to ratify
2.356

and confirm these Orders in Council in order that the object which we had in view may be carried out for the period for which the Order in Council was to operate.
If this is still a war year, would not every year in the history of any nation be a war year in order to conserve thrift?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think it very desirable in every year, as my hon. friend has said, that thrift should be promoted and resources conserved; but this is peculiarly a war year because of the enormous continuing expenditure of the Dominion Government for purposes arising out of or connected with the war and demobilization.

I would like to say one word, and in doing so do not wish to be placed in the position of opposing the resolution of the Acting Prime Minister. My ohief complaint is that it does not go far enough-that if it is intended to prevent importation of intoxicating liquor into a province, it should go further and prevent possession. I submit it would be within the power of this Government to do that. I say also that having regard to the attitude of Ontario that I entirely agree with everything that has been said with reference to giving effect to the wishes of that province.
I submit it has been known that this legislation was coming before the House, and it would possibly be of interest to the members to know, not so much what Sir William Hearst thought of this legislation at the time the original Order in Council was passed, but what the views of the Government of Ontario now are, with reference tc the extension of that legislation for a further period of twelve months.
We have heard a lot about conscription at various times-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order, the hon. member for Winnipeg Centre (Mr. Andrews) has the floor.

Further the report-says:
An exhausting and worrying day may leave a condition of tension and irritability which interferes with appetite and digestion; and in such a condition, and in some persons, it may be that wine or other dilute form of alcohol, taken with the evening meal, will assist the assimilation of food. Again, persons who have overworked to such an extent that they have become too tired to rest may be enabled to sleep when they have taken a small amount of alcohol, (p. 127.)
Gentlemen, those findings are exactly in accord with my own experience, which now extend over some years.
Oh, oh.

I am a father and a grandfather, and I have found by experience that some things agree with me and others do not-I have tried them all. The point I wish to make, Mr. Chairman, is that after a man reaches my time of life he knows pretty well what agrees with him and what does not. If I take coffee for a week I am sick; if I take a little whisky and water with my meals, then everything is all right. It does annoy me when somebody else comes along and tells me what I must drink, and would force me to follow his orders just because he happens to be in a majority. There is a little too much paternalism about that to please me.
I have given medical reasons and my own experience. I will now give the historical reasons. I claim, Mr. Chairman, that the race has not deteriorated under this alcoholic treatment that it has had for many years. No man who saw the "beer-sodden Englishman" at work on the other side can argue that it was too dangerous a drink that he had been taking; and one remembers in 1916 going to that "whisky-sodden Scotland," where every man able to march was on his way towards Flanders; and certainly in regard to the "wine-bibbing Frenchman" one remembers Verdun- "They shall not pass." Are we going to bar from this country the drink of those virile men? I know Canadians can stand it and do good work on it.
It has been pointed out to me by many of my correspondents that it is a very serious moral question. I fail to see that it has anything to do with morality. I have only to point hon. members to the unspeakable Turk, who has been a teetotaller all his days, and rather a mess he has made of it.
I would just say one word as to the rum ration in the army which has been criticised rather severely by the extreme teetotallers. In my humble opinion it saved tens of thousands of our men from the grave, and perhaps worse. After a man has been out in the water all night and comes in chilled to the marrow, there is no place in the wet trench where he can run up and down to stimulate his circulation preparatory to going to sleep. A little shot of rum at that time restores his circulation and soothes his nerves, and he gets to sleep without any trouble.
I have some notes about the "swing oi the pendulum," but I do not need to tell you about that. If you go too far the pendulum inevitably swings back the other way. But I would say one word as to the danger of going to extremes, and that is
*

the subterranean traffic which has already been mentioned. It is everywhere springing up, and it is a frightful price to pay for temperance; indeed it is too big a price to pay if you are going to build up a body of law breakers.
My hon. friend from Brandon (Mr. Whidden) when he was talking on this subject recently-I am sorry he is not in his seat to-day; he is unavoidably detained -said we should be the dumping ground of the worst elements and the worst type of business men of the North American continent. He was referring to the possible situation if Canada went v, et and the United States went dry. I understand that the hon. gentleman lived over there for some years, and is therefore probably better posted than I am, because my visits have been few and far between. But every time I have gone over there I have met some of the best business and professional men imaginable, and I do not remember one who did not take "a little drop" for his stomach's sake. When my hon. friend was talking I could not help thinking, as I remembered the moderate men I had met over there, that I would be tempted to trade off the hon. member and all his followers for them, and give fifty cents to boot. But on second thoughts, Mr. Chairman, I concluded I would not do that; and on third thoughts I decided that probably these extreme men were filling a very useful purpose in life, because unless we had extremists at the top and the bottom there would he no sane middle course for this Government to pursue.

We have heard a good deal of talk in the last year or two about conscription of wealth,, and now we are confronted with conscription of liquor in our homes. I wonder if the hon. member who advocated that will be inclined to inject a little socialistic doctrine as well and distribute the liquor at present in bond, or how else does he Isuppose the Government will be able to dispose of the liquor if it is all taken over from its present owners?
The point I wish to raise is the point raised by the hon. member for London (Mr. Cronyn)-the making of wine in Ontario for export. There has been a lot of talk in this House about reconstruction, about fostering our industries and improving them as much as possible. I see no reason why this Ontario wine should not be transported to Quebec to meet the requirements of that province, as that province has decided to have beer and wine, and

in the event of Ontario in the near future voting to follow suit a great industry would spring up in the Niagara district, where the grapes are grown. I think no objection should be taken to this clause for allowing the manufacture and export of native wine.
As to the breweries in Ontario being allowed to manufacture beer to meet the requirements of Quebec or any other province that may vote wet, I see no objection to it. At the present time the Ontario brewers are manufacturing supplies to meet medical needs, and I cannot see what objection can be taken to their being allowed to go a little further to meet the needs of a sister province, and so being prepared, perhaps in the very near future, to meet the needs of Ontario itself. I think that might well have been included in this motion.
I do not see anything in this resolution about permitting the importation of wine for sacramental purposes.

This item is to carry on improvements that have been in progress for some time. The amount asked for is not sufficient to complete the works; in fact, it will take very much more than this. The intention is to start the extension of a breakwater on the Port Arthur side and to continue the construction of a revetment wall near the terminals of the Grand Trunk Pacific on the Fort William side of the harbour. We believe that this is about as much money as will be expended during the coming year, although it is possible that an additional amount will be asked for in the Supplementary Estimates.
St. John harbour-Improvements, $750,000.

This is to carry on improvements in the harbour of St. John. The work, which is under contract, involves also the construction of a dry dock. The amount of the vote will really be applied to harbour improvements. The harbour improvements and the dry dock are both under contract with the same company, the St. John Dry Dock and 'Shipbuilding Company, really the Canada Dredging Company, which has carried out works at Port Arthur and Fort William and at many places in Canada.
At what stage of completion is the dry dock, and what harbour improvements are being carried on by this company?

The original contract
was given in 1912, and provided for the construction of a breakwater, the dredging of a very large area in what is called Courtenay Bay, and the construction of a dry dock. Up to the time that the contract was assigned to the new company it had been carried on by the Norton-Griffiths Company, and about $4,000,000 had been expended on the harbour improvements and about $900,000 on the dry dock. The dry dock is being built under the Dry Dock Subsidies Act. It will cost at least $5,500,-
000 and the contractors are to receive not a subsidy of four and one half per cent, but interest on an amount up to $5,500,000 at four and one half per cent for thirty-five years. The principal of the bonds, of course, has to be taken care of by the contractors themselves. When the work is completed the harbour improvements will belong to the Government and the dry dock will belong to the company; so that two distinct propositions are incorporated in the same contract. Work is progressing on the dry dock.
The contract calls for the construction of a dry dock and of a ship repairing plant. The ship repairing plant itself comes under The Dry Dock Subsidy Act, but the money will be furnished by the company and not by the 'Government. It involves an expenditure of, I think, $3,250,000. The company are also laying out a big shipyard, but that is entirely their own affair; we have nothing to do with it whatever; it has nothing to do with the dry dock subsidy contract, nor with the harbour works. Under the contract the dry dock was to- be ready for operation in the summer of 1922, but we believe from the progress which they are making and from the reports of our engineers that it will be ready for operation in the summer of 1921.

What size ships will it be able to accommodate?
Mr. iCARVEiLL: The largest ship afloat to-day. In fact, it will be one of the largest dry docks in existence. It is 1,150 feet in length, 125 feet wide, 100 feet on the sil'l, with 40 feet of water at high tide. In every way it will be one of the most up-to-date dry docks in the world. There are only three others on the American continent that will at all compare with it. First, the 'Champlain dry dock at Levis; secondly, the dook_at Boston, and, thirdly, the dock at the Atlantic entrance to the Panama 'Canal. It will be equipped with the most up-to-date machinery, and, with the ship repairing plant, it will go a long way towards being a shipbuilding plant. I shall gladly give any other information if the members wish it.

No doubt 'there was a written contract between the Government and the company for the building of this dry dock under the Dry Docks. Act. That Act is a very short one, and I should like to know if there is anything in the contract itself conserving the rights of the public as to the use of this dock when completed. The dry dock, of course, will be privately owned, but it will be the public who will

utilize the dock. Otherwise, the dry dock could not do business. Now we can always trust Government-owned utilities of this kind, because they are the property of the people, and governments have to cater to the wishes of the people. But in the case of a private-owned institution it is well that there should be some control over the fees that they can charge against the tonnage that is put into the dock for repairs. Has any such provision been made in the contract?

vogue to-day in the building of docks, one being . for the Government themselves to. build the dock, which means a tremendous outlay, and there is always the great problem as to what will be done with the dock after completion. If we can get docks constructed by companies under the dry docks subsidy and under Government control and subject to Government ratification of fees that can be charged, they are relieved of a very large expenditure, because the 41 per cent extended over a period of thirty-five years is a very small matter compared with the initial cost of building a firshclass dry dock, and the Government is also relieved of its operation. My hon. friend is enough of a business man to know that there is not much use in talking about operating a dry dock and making money out of it. That cannot be done by the Government. If an up-to-date business concern own the dock, it is in their interest to get business. There will be no question of discrimination, and the only question that will weigh with them will be the getting of enough business to make it a paying concern. Personally, I am very much in favour of the construction of docks under subsidy, but up to the present time we have had very poor success, and- I do not believe it is possible to get any other docks built in Canada under subsidy without an increase in the subsidy. My own judgment would be that the second-class dry dock should receive subsidy up to 4J per cent for thirty-five years upon cost the same as first-class docks. If that were done, dry docks of the second class could be provided in a number of places in Canada without the Government actually paying for them.
