I do not know, Mr. Chairman, that I have anything further to say.

Why is this dredging tied up altogether? There does not seem naturally to he any particular connection between the building of a dry dock and dredging at Courtenay bay. While the dry dock is a fixed proposition, years one way or the other will not change the situation, and I think it is perhaps dangerous to make a contract for dredging that will extend over a great many years. Labour and everything is high, but after some years we can hope that matters will be such that the proposed services will be obtained at a cheaper rate than contracts made during the past few years. I would like to know what number of years this dredging arrangement covers, and what amount, apart from the dry dock, the dredging involves.

My hon. friend's question would be a very apt one if a new contract had been made, but I think he will be surprised to learn that this contract was entered into in March, 1912, and that the work is going on under the prices prevailing then. There is no public work in Canada in which the Government is getting the work done under conditions existing in 1912. Tenders were called for this work, which was advertised perhaps as no other public work was ever advertised in Canada. Every district engineer in Canada had a copy of the plans and specifications, and there were notices running for between two and three months in all the big newspapers. In addition to this, a copy of the plans and specifications was deposited in the Office of the High Commissioner in London. Three tenders were received, all from English firms, the lowest tender being from the firm of Norten-Griffiths Company, Limited, for between eight and nine million dollars, including the dredging of a certain specified area, the building of piers, and the construction of a breakwater. The second part of the tender concerned the construction of a dry dock. When I came into the department I found that about four million dollars' worth of work had

been done on the harbour part of it. Work had proceeded. on the dry dock, but no subsidy contract had been entered into. The only subsidy contract that was ever signed was that signed about a year ago, with the present company, that is, Norton Griffiths Company Limited. While they did a large amount of work on the dry dock they never bad a subsidy contract. Now there is a subsidy contract under the law, and instead of going on and increasing the work we have decreased it. For instance, the channel leading from the main St. John harbour into Courtenay bay was to be 32 feet at low water. That involved some submarine rock work. We have eliminated all the rock work in the channel, and the channel itself will be dredged down to about 22 feet. We have reduced the cost of the channel by hundreds of thousands of dollars and are not doing any submarine rock dredging in the channel, my view being-and perhaps I am taking my own engineering opinions in regard to this work-that no ship will ever dock in St. John at low wdter. It is well known to many members of the Committee that St. John labours under a great disadvantage, having a high tide of 25 feet normal and 27 feet in spring tides. I do not believe that any ship will ever go into that channel to dock at low tide. Ships do not do it to-day but wait at the bar until at least half tide. Under the circumstances, we thought we could save considerable money and eliminated a lot of that dredging. The construction of the four piers was provided for in the original contract. We have eliminated that from the present contract because we do not consider it absolutely necessary. We want the basin and the entrance to the dry dock completed, but there is a clause in the contract which provides that whenever the present contractors are called upon to complete the piers they must do so under the prices in the contract of 1912. So that if we attempted to call for new tenders to carry on this work under present conditions, it would cost at least 50 per cent more than at the present time, and probably higher than that.
Did the minister not inform the House last year that this dredging contract had been cancelled?

I informed the House
that I was not sure whether we were going on with the work or not. When I came into the department, it was contended by certain people that the contract was cancelled.
I had no hesitation in saying that the coni' .Mr. Carvell.J
tract had not been cancelled. Just before I made that statement I had referred the matter to the Department of Justice. Within about a month, or when the Supplementary Estimates came up, I was asked the question again and I said that we were going on with the work and in the meantime I received a notification from the Justice Department that the contract was not cancelled, that it was still alive. On that assurance I ratified the assignment of the contract by the Norton Griffiths Company to the St. John Shipbuilding Company, or rather consented to it.
What amount is involved in the subsidy?

You can figure it out
yourself; it is 4J per cent on $5,500,000 for thirty-five years. No part of this has been paid because the work has not progressed to the point where 1 feel justified in guaranteeing the bonds. Just as soon as $1,000,000 has been expended, if the company want it, I shall ask council to guarantee the bonds. They have to finance it themselves. At the present time I do not believe they could sell these bonds for sixty, if for anything at all. However, they can take the bonds if they want to because they are entitled to them; that is entirely their affair. They finance it and we do the harbour work. The basin, which will be provided, will cover about 80 acres, and notwithstanding the fact that some derogatory tilings have been said about it, it is going to be one of the finest harbours in Canada when it is completed. It is true that we have a very high tide to contend with; it is true that nature has not been kind to the port of St. John, but geographically it is in the place where the business is being done. The people of St. John have had the courage and energy to do what no other city or community in Canada has done. They started out to do a transatlantic business and to make St. John a great national port, and they have put up between $2,250,000 and $2,500,000 of their own money, carrying out the work, financing it and taking hold of it themselves. It is urged that the Government should take this port over and put it under a commission. I believe it ought to be done. But, however, they have spent their own money and the Dominion of Canada has spent less on the harbour of St. John than on any other harbour in Canada of its size and importance. There is more business done at the port of St. John than in any other port in Canada save Montreal; in the las't fiscal year $221,000,000 worth of business was done through the port of St. John. The

business there does not start until after November. The armistice was signed in November, but since that time $175,000,000 worth was done through that port. It is the natural port of Canada in the winter time. There is no use of saying that there are some mud banks and that for that reason we cannot go on. The mud banks may be there, but it is the duty of any man who occupies this position to see that that port is fairly dealt with and that it is put in a position to carry on the business that they have there in the winter time. We must either do that or hand it over to Portland or Boston. It is true that we have the port of Halifax, the finest port probably on the American coast. I am sure 'there is nothing like it on the whole Atlantic coast.
It is not better than Sydney harbour, is it?

It is far better-and I do not want to say anything derogatory of Sydney harbour. Halifax has a magnificent harbour, the like of which hardly exists anywhere else in the world. But, unfortunately, it is 200 miles farther away from the business* of Canada than 'St. John, and notwithstanding all the war business that has been going through Halifax it has not done a quarter of the business that has been done through St. John. That is on account of the geographical position of St. John.
The three greatest harbours in the world are Halifax, Sydney and Melbourne. The great man who made that pronouncement did not undertake to differentiate between them.
What about Vancouver?

The minister said that Halifax was 200 miles farther east than St. John. Is there any difference in the freight rate between a point in Ontario or Quebec on export shipments by St. John or Halifax?
Mr. CARVEIiL: There is one cent per hundred pounds. Boston, Portland and St. John enjoy the same rate. There is an advance of one cent as against Halifax.
Toronto harbour-improvements, $500,000.
Mr. THOMAiS FOSTER: Hoes the minister know the condition of Toronto harbour? Last year the matter came up before the House, but since that time there have been many changes in connection with the hafbour due to storm destruction. Perhaps the minister remembers that about 1897 the south shore of the island was in a very dangerous condition and it was possible that the whole of the island would be destroyed. The Board of Trade and City Council, realizing the situation, made representations to the Government at that time and it was pointed out that if something was not done there was a possibility of the entire island being destroyed. The Government realized that if that should happen there would be no protection for the riparian rights of the Government along the harbour and it would become a very expensive proposition for them. The Board of Trade and City Council entered into negotiations with the Government. The Government undertook to spend $200,000 if the city would expend $100,000; so that about $300,000 was expended at that time to protect the south shore of the island. That gave temporary protection but in a year or two it was found that the protection was not substantial. They had to adopt another method and again expend more money to protect the south shore. They protected that part of the island. Now we realize, and the Government realize too, that there must be further protection. The minister will remember that the Government agreed to expend about $6,000,000, the Harbour Commission $13,000,000, and the city of Toronto $2,000,000, making an investment in harbour improvements in Toronto of about $21,000,000. There have been, I think, three Orders in Council passed committing the Government to this expenditure. I have here a copy of Order in Council No. 1,426, passed on June 10th, 1913, which describes some of the protective works that were required and which form a part of the contract. Section (b) on page 5 contains this description:
The construction of a crib 'breakwater, approximate 18,600 feet long, to protect the lake shore west of the western entrance to the harbour.
Then section (c) of the same Order in Council relates to:
The construction of a seawall of pile work, approximate 17,295 feet long-, to protect the lake shore on the east side of the east entrance to the harbour.
Under the authority of this Order in Council the work was undertaken, and in the western section about 4,100 feet of crib sub-structure has been built at a cost of about $187,000, which is now being protected by concrete coping. I may say that the greater part of this work was destroyed by a storm. The Harbour Commissioners of Toronto spent about $1,240,000 on this part of the western section, and already about $100,000 damage has been caused to the western section of the cribwork on the

lake shore. This estimate of damages was made in the early part of the present year, and within the last week a further destruction of the work on this part of the harbour shore has taken place.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
When the Committee rose at six o'clock we were considering item 110 on page 69 of the Estimates. The item had been considered sub-item by subitem and we had reached:
Toronto harbour-Improvements.
Mr. Foster had the floor.

I would like to say to the Minister of Public Works that the engineer of the Harbour Commission estimated the damage done in the early part of the year along the shore of Humber Bay at about $100,000. Since that estimate was made we have had some very heavy southeast storms which have caused a further loss of $10,000 or $15,000. About two weeks ago I had occasion to go along the shore and I noticed a great change since my former visit by reason of the washing away of the reclaimed land, showing that if something is not done immediately there is going to be a further tremendous loss for the Harbour Commission and the city that the Government will no doubt have to make good. If the work had been completed a year or two ago, as we [Mr, Thomas Foster.!
expected, the Harbour Commission and the city would have saved about $75,000 per annum as well as this loss of $115,000, which makes it a very serious proposition for them.
The cribs that had been, completed for section 5 have been lying for almost two years exposed to the weather and they are rapidly deteriorating, and, consequently, a heavy loss is being sustained. To protect this work and to place three 100-foot cribs on section 5, would cost, it is estimated, about $152,448. Surely it would be good business and economy to spend this amount to make use of those cribs and to protect this reclaimed land.
In 1918-19 the Estimates provided for some $500,000, and about $80,000 or $100,000 of that was to meet some drawback, which would reduce the amount intended to be used to complete the ship canal to about $420,000. Whether that has been completed and this work protected or not I do not know, but I expect the minister will be able to explain if there is any balance unexpended. If the Government would expend about $496,180 protection would be provided for reclaimed land that has cost about $1,240,193 to reclaim. If that is done I understand from the engineer that it would not matter so much if the work was then allowed to stand for some time until the minister found it more advantageous to carry it to completion, I also understand from the engineer that the substructure that was put down about two years ago has been for the most part destroyed. I drew the attention of the minister to that fact last year, and I understood him to undertake to place in his Supplementary Estimates some $150,000 to protect that work. I do not know whether he is carrying that forward, but it seems to me false economy to have $187,000 worth of work destroyed for want of an additional expenditure of $150,000 to complete it, and to defer the expenditure of some $400,000 to protect $1,240,000 worth of work. So, while I give the minister a great deal of credit for his policy of economy, yet in a case of this kind I would say that to refrain from making the additional necessary expenditure is not economy and does not show good judgment.
According to this Order in Council the Government is committed to an expenditure of some $6,000,000. I think three Orders in Council were passed by the Government in reference to this expenditure. There was to be a sea wall built from the western channel crossing Humber bay and from the

eastern channel to Woodbine avenue, or a little, further east. Nothing has been done on the eastern section and as the result there has been further destruction of Kew Beach park, a very valuable section. I understand from the city engineer that it will cost 850,000 to protect a small part of the shore there. In the last two or three days a very heavy storm from the southeast has taken away a considerable section of the southwest portion of the island. According to a report I have received two or three large trees and a couple of hundred feet of concrete walk were washed away, and the water is now very close to some valuable residential property. Surely it is time that immediate action was taken to avoid further destruction of these improvements which have cost a great deal of money, and as the Government is committed to this expenditure I would urge the minister to take the necessary steps to have the work completed.
If the minister has made an inspection of the harbour and of these shores he must appreciate the value of the part of the island of which I speak. This year the water is higher than usual and when there is a strong southeast wind there is often great destruction on the island. We have had an evidence of that within the last three days.
I see that the minister is asking for only $500,000 this year as against $702,000 last year. I shall be glad to hear him explain how he proposes to spend that $500,000; I cannot conceive that it will give the protection that is desirable and necessary. A good many years ago we undertook to protect a section of the west side of the eastern channel by building a breakwater there; that has helped to protect that section of the island. But that work has been there over thirty years and has become partly destroyed. If this sea-wall that the Government has committed itself to is not very soon placed in its proper position, the needed protection to that part of the island will not be given, because the old breakwater will not last much longer. On this section of the island there are some valuable summer residences and the erection of a breakwater along this entire shore from the east 'to the west should be immediately undertaken. Perhaps the minister will give us some information regarding this proposed expehditure and tell us whether he intends to put in the Supplementary Estimates the amount necessary to carry out the policy to which the Government is committed in connection with this work.

My hon. friend has very fairly indeed stated the condition of affairs from his standpoint, and also from the standpoint of fact. He referred first to the protection of the island and to the fact that a good many years ago the Dominion Government erected a number of groins along that portion of the island in front of Toronto harbour lying westward of what is called the Eastern Passage. I was in that vicinity a year and a half ago but I did not inspect that portion of the work closely enough to be able to discuss it intelligently. The description, however, which the hon. member has given corresponds almost exactly with the information which I have received from the officers of the department. The protection of land in various parts of Canada from the action of the waters of rivers, lakes and the sea is a question with which I have laboured more, perhaps, since I have been Minister of Public Works than with any other question of policy. I have had applications from British Columbia, involving tremendous amounts of money, for the protection of lands in that province from the ravages of the Fraser river and other rivers in British Columbia. I have received numerous applications also from Nova Scotia, Ontario and Quebec. I do not know how many applications I have received from members of Parliament and Boards of Trade and Municipal Councils in the province of Quebec that steps be taken by the Dominion Government to take care of erosion along the river St. Lawrence. I mention these merely to show you that the problem is a very great one. I have a very strong feeling that, theoretically at least, the Federal Government ought not to be called upon to protect the land of any part of Canada from erosion. That is something that is the natural consequence of things; it is something that follows the ownership of land. But it is hard to lay down a policy founded upon principle, because all sorts of things; have been done in the past; therefore I cannot say that nothing will be done. I promised the people of Toronto a week or ten days ago that I would go there with my engineer and look into the matter; I will do so. What I call the principle with regard to this matter has been violated so many times during the last twenty-five or thirty years that I think we should consider these cases individually as we find them, and do what is right in the premises.
Now I come to the next portion of the hon. member's remarks which had reference to a scheme partly of harbour develop-

rnent, partly of shore protection and partly of the beautification of Toronto. He is correct in saying that in 1913 an agreement was made between the Dominion Government, the city of Toronto, and the Harbour Commissioners of Toronto under which certain work was to be done. The Dominion s share was a little under $6,000,000 and the Harbour, Commissioners of Toronto and the city were to spend $15,000,000. A contract was entered into with the Canadian Stewart Company for the carrying out of the Dominion Government's portion of this work. That contract was very unsatisfactory from the Government's standpoint. The work was to have been completed about the time-I think the very week-I entered the Government, but it was not nearly completed. A tremendous amount of work, involving about $600,000 or $700,000, had been done so badly that the company were compelled to tear it down and build over again.
Mr. MoKENZIE:	Can the minister explain why work involving $600,000 was permitted to proceed in such an unsatisfactory manner?

No, I cannot. I can
only say that it did proceed and that the department found it out and compelled the Stewart Company to make good. And they did make good; I think that work is the finest of its kind that I have ever looked at. I speak'now of the piles and the construction, the development generally, in Ashbridge's bay. When I visited the work in the fall of 1917 the water had been pumped out of the canal so that the character of the work could be seen. The sheetpiling was driven in so closely that you could not find a space of a quarter of an inch between the piles. So far as I could observe, everything seemed to be in perfect order. But I came into this Government with the distinct pledge that I would save every dollar that I could possibly save until the war was over. I did not close up the Toronto Harbour works, but I put on all the brakes I possibly could. My first act as Minister of Public Works was to cancel a contract for a million dollar breakwater at St. John.
I thought that a pretty good place to commence to show that I was in earnest in trying to sfilut off unnecessary expenditure was at home, and I did it, and I have received a great deal of adverse criticism for doing so. , We also closed down the works on the St. Charles river and on the Welland canal. I have closed down construction on every big work wherever I possibly could. Among the works that I par-
[Mr. Oarvell. J
tially closed down were the Toronto harbour works. I cannot agree with the figures quoted by my hon. friend, although he quotes them in good faith, having got them from the Toronto Harbour Commissioners. The commissioners have quoted the same figures to me a good many times. They have said that $100,000 of damage has been done to their work, because the Government's part of the work was not finished in the Humber Bay district. I have inspected the work at Toronto. The construction consists of a series of cribs sunk out in the lake about 300 to 400 yards from the shore. The intention is that that crib work is to be covered with cement, and a wall built higher than the waves of the lake. This will leave a sort of lagoon between the wall and the shore. The Harbour Commissioners have had a tremendous quantity of sand pumped out of the lake back against the shore, and in some places this sand is within, I suppose, 500 or 600 feet off the crib work, or perhaps less. The contention of the Harbour Commissioners is that because a concrete tap was not put on the crib work there has been a loss of the material which they have pumped back against the shore. It may be all true what they say about the damage, but I could not see it. From my homely way of looking at engineering problems, I have not been convinced that there has been the loss they state.
You will see the damage when you go back.

Undoubtedly there has been some loss. In fact, wherever works have been closed down in Canada there has been some loss. Last year there was a vote in the Supplementary Estimates for $156,000 for putting the concrete top on the cribs that had already been sunk and for sinking a further short distance of crib.
Three 100-foot cribs.

The cribs have been constructed and they are now tied up to the shore. The idea was to sink them, and we started out to do so. I called upon the contractors, the Canadian 'Stewart Company, to sink these cribs and put the concrete top on the cribs that had already been sunk. They took the ground that on account of a letter which had been written to them by the chief engineer in the fall of 1917 their contract was cancelled after a certain amount of work was done! While I did not write that letter, I take full responsibility for it. I did not know whether the contract

was cancelled or not. They said it was, and they refused to go on with the work. I submitted the matter to the Justice Department, and the Justice Department said that in their opinion the contract was cancelled. I started out to see if I could get the work done by other parties, but in view of labour conditions in Toronto and all over Canada it was not only an impossibility, but a Godsend that we could not go on with the work. At that time you could not get men to perform work of that kind, so I simply accepted the situation and allowed the matter to stand, and nothing was done so far as the cribs were concerned. That is the reason why the total amount of the money voted last year was not expended. In the letter which had been written to the Canadian-Stewart Company we pointed out that they were to do certain work, amounting, I think, to a little over $300,000. They carried out the work in so far as we instructed them. Then they claimed their contract was closed and we were very glad, indeed, that they did claim it was closed. We also claimed that it was closed, so there is no hard feeling on our side. Now they claim that the contract was not closed, and they want half a million dollars damages because the contract was closed down. I want to say here what I have said to them, that the only way they will get their half million dollars will be at the tail end of a lawsuit which will go just as far as the courts of this country will allow it to go.
As to the work in contemplation, there is an item in the Estimates of $500,000 which we estimate is as much money as can possibly be expended on Toronto harbour during the coming season. We may be a little out, but I think not. The work to be performed consists in putting the top on the cribs which have been sunk, sinking the 300 feet of cribs which have already been built and putting a concrete top on them, and finishing up the work in Ashbridge's Bay. Now, $500,000 will not do all this work. We estimate that it will take $800,000, or, perhaps, a little more to finish up the work I have described.
It must be remembered that the Toronto harbour proposition consists of two portions. The development of Ashbridge's bay is purely a harbour proposition, and in my judgment a very good one. Ashbridge's bay is a great level sand bank in front of the city of Toronto, covering some thousands of acres which at certain times of the year are practically inundated; at all events, the water comes almost to the top. When the water goes down, the land will be a foot or two out of the wmter. The idea was to
dig a canal 400 feet wide and about half a mile or a little longer in length right through the centre of the bay. The material that is pumped out of the canal, and out of the big turning basin at the far end of it, is thrown back over the land, and the harbour commissioners are pumping sand out of the lake as well. They are building up the land on either side of the canal for industrial sites, and I have no doubt that Ashbridge's bay will be one of the greatest industrial sites in Canada in the near future; in fact, large concerns have already located there. For instance, the Imperial Munitions Board established a very large plant there.
Who will own that land ?

The Toronto Harbour Commissioners. We are simply carrying on the navigation work. The spoil has to be taken care of in some way, and' it is a great deal cheaper to pump it back on the land than to take it out and dump it in the lake. When this work is completed there will be a canal 400 feet wide, and from one-half to three-quarters of a mile in length, with a turning basin about 1,100 feet square at the end of it, with a breathing space between the turning basin and the island. This will avoid any trouble over stagnant water, and will make the place clean and sanitary. I repeat, I think it will become a great industrial centre.
The other portion of the work is not in any sense a navigation proposition. It is building this breakwater on either side of the city of Toronto, about four miles in length on the western side, and three and-a-half miles on the eastern side.
I have never seen the canal the minister has referred to. Will the minister explain why he is endeavouring to improve navigation by cutting through this flat?

I am not doing it, because it was done before I came in. I examined the work, however, and I looked upon it as a splendid proposition. The idea is to provide a water front on Ashbridge's bay of over half a mile, and my hon. friend will remember that there are no tides in Toronto harbour as in his part of the country. The canal is 24 feet deep, which will take care of any vessel which goes through the new Welland canal. Taking both sides, there will be a series of wharves extending about a mile and-a-half. On both sides of this canal and around the turning basin will be industrial sites. It may be a large contribution to the in-

dustrial life of Toronto, but it is a transportation proposition pure and simple from the standpoint of the Government and one which requires no defence, because if any one went and inspected it he would come to the conclusion that it is a real transportation problem.
It is really a proposition to reclaim land.

Yes, it is in a sense.
Without a doubt it is a proposition to reclaim land, but at the same time it is making available a mile and a half water front which will be of inestimable value.

Is wharf accommodation
needed now?

I do not know. They
have considerable wharf accommodation in Toronto, but my friend must remember that the Welland canal when completed will mean a revolution in the water-borne transportation of the whole of lake Ontario, and in fact down the St. Lawrence river as far as Prescott. Then following that comes the next great problem of canalizing the St. Lawrence river.
Should not these reclaimed lands pay for the expenditure involved in these improvements?

That might be. I can
only say that as I understand the contract that is not the case. I have nothing to defend and nothing to conceal; I state the facts as they are. The Government might have said: "We will retain the ownership in these lands and will lease them." But they did not. I do not want to attempt to disguise the thing at all.

You do retain a section
on the west part of the channel?

We retain a small section but the great majority goes over to the Harbour Commission. As regards the remainder of the work, it would mean the construction of a sea wall of about seven or eight miles in length altogether if the whole scheme were carried out. At present we are carrying out only a small portion of the scheme, and it will certainly be a most beautiful place. The city of Toronto is reclaiming land along the lake front but is doing it at its own expense and of course will own it, but I do not think that even gentlemen from Toronto will claim that that is a transportation proposition as much as Ashbridge's bay.
Is it the intention of the Government to continue with the work on that seven or eight miles until completed?
Not this year.
In succeeding years?

That will be a matter of policy later on. I have no announcement to make except that we propose this year putting on the concrete tops on the cribs that are now sunk and on 300 feet that we intend to sink. We also purpose to finish the Ashbridge's bay proposition. There is no use disguising the 'fact that there is a contract between the Government of Canada, the City of Toronto and the Harbour Commissioners of Toronto to carry out the whole scheme which will involve at least $7,000,000.
When was the contract made?
The Order in Council was passed in 1913 and I believe the contract was made in October of the same year.
Is there a time limit for its completion?
It was to have been completed in October, 1917.
How much has been spent to date?
Practically two and a half millions.
What portion was the Government to expend?

A little less than $6,000,000. The city of Toronto and the Harbour Commissioners-which is the same thing because their bonds are guaranteed by the city of Toronto-were to expend about $15,000,000. The total expenditure was to be about $20,000,000. I think that if we go on and finish our part of it it will cost about $7,000,000 when completed. We have now expended about $2,500,000 and are asking for an appropriation of $500,000 at the present time which will be used in putting the concrete tops on these piers and finishing the Ashbridge's bay part of the work as far as it will extend. It will take about $850,000 to finish up what we have in prospect at the present time.
Can the minister give the Committee an idea of the water-borne exports from and imports into Toronto?

No, I cannot do so, but I do not 'think they are anything like

what they will be in the immediate future. I am a great believer in water transportation. I believe that the people will devote their attention to waterborne transportation, especially on inland waters, to a much greater extent in the future than in the past, and when the W elland canal is completed Toronto will be one of the most important seaports on the Great Lakes. Toronto is not an important seaport to-day for the reason that the big ships which navigate from the head of the lakes to Port Colborne cannot come to Toronto and therefore the shipping in Toronto is confined to the 14-foot draught vessel which can get through the Welland canal or down the St. Laiwrence. But with a city having the manufacturing and trade possibilities of Toronto, there cannot be any question that when the Welland canal is completed Toronto harbour will be entirely different from what it is to-day. And the Government are not only entitled but compelled to provide necessary transportation facilities in Toronto for the future as they have done in Montreal, St. John, Halifax or any other port. I will admit at once, however, that if the Welland canal were not going to be deepened the Ash-bridge's Bay proposition would not in my opinion be justifiable because there would not be traffic to justify it.

When will the Welland canal be finished?
Mr. CARVEiLL: I hope in about three years, but that is not in my department. It seems to me that it should be completed in three years. This work, I presume, will be completed sometime in 1920. In other words, Ashbridge's bay will be completed a year or two before the Welland canal.

It is important to know how the system of connecting Montreal with say Toronto is to be completed. When we get to the eastern end of the Welland canal what position are we in between there and Montreal?

We are then in a position to reach the largest boats that will come down the Great Lakes as far east as Kingston and there should be good business done as far as Prescott. It would be possible to navigate the St. Lawrence as far as Prescott, although I understand it would require some work in the river channel between Kingston and Prescott in order to make it navigable for large boats. But the moment the Welland canal is completed the biggest boats that ply on Lake Erie and Lake Superior at present will be able to
come down not only to Toronto but to Kingston, and any man who looks at the map and who travels over the country and knows anything about its business will realize that Toronto will be a very different port after the Welland canal is completed from what it is now.
I am afraid the minister is beginning a big expenditure at the wrong end. I think he should begin in navigable water and continue going inland.

There are various views about that phase of the question. Of course 1 did not begin it, although I not only do not have to justify it; but I am heartily in accord with the Ashbridge's bay portion of the Toronto development. There is another thing we must remember. It is all very well to say: "You have started here, whereas you should have begun somewhere else." It means a great many millions of dollars, indeed tens of millions of dollars, in order to make it possible for a 21 or 22-foot boat to navigate from Montreal to Toronto, and I do not think we would be justified in holding up navigation as far as Kingston pending the completion of the bigger scheme. The Welland canal, we know, can be completed and will be completed within a reasonable time. But the other I will not say is very far in the future, but it will re*quire a great deal of study and investigation and the expenditure of a tremendous amount of money before it is finished. In view of this, I am not sure that the Government were not right in starting on the Welland canal. There is always the contention that the construction of the Welland canal is going to benefit the American lake ports, and that wheat will be brought to Oswego on lake Ontario, and sent by canal thence to New York. I am not in a position to discuss that point intelligently and I do not know that it plays a very great part here. I repeat that the Ashbridge's bay proposition is a sound one and will not be completed very much before it is used and used in a very profitable manner.

The minister has been putting figures before us which I cannot help regarding as simply appalling in view of the financial condition of the country. Has the Government in continuing or launching upon this scheme-I am not prepared to say whether it is a new scheme or the continuation of an old one-made any calculation of what is the probable use these great public works necessitating the



expenditure of tremendous amounts of money will be? We are being asked to pass these Estimates and the responsibility is upon all of us for the expenditure of these very large sums. I would feel easier in my conscience if the minister could give us some idea of what the result of this expenditure is going to be.

I do not know that 1
can give my hon. friend very much information along that line. This is no scheme launched by this Government. The Welland canal and Toronto harbour works were launched before the war. With a debt of $325,000,000 or $300,000,000 and with buoyant revenues, there was no trouble about expending $10,000,000 upon a transportation problem. We had the money to do it with.
The situation is absolutely different now.

It has changed; there
is no man in Canada who realizes that so much as I do. I took the trouble on the Address to sound a note of warning and sometimes I think I did not get very much assistance or sympathy from the House.

We made all the use
we could of the hon. gentleman's statement.

I tried to point out
someihing about the financial condition as I viewed it. I have not launched out upon any new scheme and I am going to be pretty careful how I do launch out upon any new scheme. But I think I have some idea cf business, and when I find in my department a public work upon which some mi'lions of dollars have been expended, and which is absolutely useless until it is finished. I see nothing to do but to finish it in so far as you can. I hope my hon. friend will not charge me with launching upon any new schemes involving the expenditure of large amounts until I know what the results are going to be. But in a case like this I see nothing else to do. We have spent $2,500,000 on the Ashbridge's bay proposition which is two-thirds or three-fourths completed. We have to finish it; otherwise the money we have put into it will be lost. I agree that we ought not to launch upon any new scheme involving the expenditure of large amounts unless we have well considered the business phase of it in order to see if it is going to give us a revenue.
Will the minister tell us if it is his intention to finish up the damming of the St. Charles river at Quebec?

There is no vote in the Estimates for that. The trouble with the St. Charles river proposition at Quebec is a very simple one. The scheme is to construct a dam across the mouth of the river where it empties into the St. Lawrence. There were to be two entrances from the St. Lawrence up into the basins of the St. Charles river. That was to create practically a lake 12 or 14 feet higher than the ordinary level of the river at low tide and, to some extent, higher than the level would be at high tide. The sewage of at least three-quarters of the city of Quebec enters into the St. Charles river above the location of this dam and before the work was started an agreement was made with the city of Quebec by which they were to provide for the sewage. There was to be a big trunk sewer constructed by which the sewage would be emptied into the S't. Lawrence river around and below the dam at the mouth of the St. Charles. It will cost probably $2,000,000. I suppose they had some trouble about financing it during the war but no attempt has been made to take care of that sewage. They have refused to go on with the work until something is done about the sewage. If you build a dam across the St. Charles river and dump the sewage of 75,000 or 80,000 people into the river for a year you will have a pest house; you could not live alongside of it. I would not take the responsibility of consenting to go on with the work until something was done about the sewage. With this I take the same ground that I have taken in regard to St. John and other places. We have about $1,750,000 invested in the St. Charles river work at the present time and it will take another $1,000,000 to finish it. The money we have expended is absolutely lost until the work is completed but I cannot go on and complete it until something is done to protect the health of the city of Quebec.

The hon. member for
Brome (Mr. McMaster) finds the figures indicating expenditures at Toronto harbour appalling.
I did not say Toronto harbour. It was the whole thing, the Welland canal, Toronto harbour and other works, that I referred to. I was not especially referring to Toronto.

Then the hon. gentleman's interjection occurred at an inop-

portune time. One would naturally conclude that he was appalled at the expenditure at Toronto. I am glad to know that that was not the case because I have never seen any indication of .panic on the part of the hon. gentleman when an expenditure was to be made in the vicinity of Montreal. He could stand any amount of expenditure down there without turning a hair.

He has not got any
hair.

Then my remark is
incontrovertible; it cannot be questioned. There is another thing that I want to refer to. The minister would have us believe that a new era of economy, retrenchment and general saving opened up at the time that he entered office. Time and again he has assured us that he is not to be held responsible for any expenditures previous to that event. I have sat in this House for a number of years and I think I am [DOT]correct in stating that when these expenditures were entered upon at Toronto *and other parts of the country they went through without any very serious opposition from the gentlemen who are now sitting on the other side of the House and from gentlemen who are now sitting on this side of the House. The general principle was accepted then. These expenditures, as a general thing, have been justified. In [DOT]regard to the St. Lawrence route, I did mot hear the minister mention anything about the carrying of grain from lake Ontario down through to Montreal. I would almost infer from his remarks that Toronto was to be the trans-shipping point for grain coming down in big freighters when the Welland canal is completed.
I hope that is not the intention of the Government 'because it seems to me that when that time arrives the proper point for trans-shipping the grain carried in these large vessels is the city of Kingston.

My hon. friend certainly misunderstood me. I made no reference, or even a hint, to a possible trans-shipment of grain at Toronto; I don't believe that will ever happen. What I was talking about was the expansion of the general business of Toronto.

Then we are in entire agreement on that point. I do not think the leader of the Opposition has the right idea When he suggests that the proper way to arrange this line of transportation would be to begin at the lower end, at Montreal I presume he means, and canalize the St.
151J
Lawrence. Before you undertook to make provision for transporting the grain available for the route from the Welland canal to Kingston or Prescott-before you could possibly complete an enterprise of that kind-that grain would be diverted from Canadian channels to American routes entirely. It does seem to me that something should be done, and done right away, to .make provision at Kingston for the transshipment of the grain which will come down when the new Welland canal is completed. Kingston is the natural point for trans-shipment, because the grain can be loaded there into any kind of vessel at all [DOT]by reason of the fact that the route from Kingston to Montreal lies in sheltered water. A vessel which could not stand the heavy seas or storms likely to be encountered on lake Ontario would therefore be quite capable of engaging in the carrying trade from Kingston to Montreal. In my opinion the Government should not wait until the new Welland canal is completed before making provision at Kingston for the trans-shipping of the grain which the big freighters will carry as far as that point. Although I speak from 'the standpoint of an Ontario man, and one who resides in the neighbourhood of Kingston,, the advocacy of this idea is not confined to eastern men alone. I think I am right in saying that some years ago the grain growers of the West, when looking forward to the completion of the Welland canal, suggested that a Government elevator, somewhat similar to the one which is now in existence at Port Colborne, should be built at Kingston. I hope the Government will not delay in providing the necessary facilities at that port because if delay takes place we are going to lose the carriage of that grain; the Americans will promptly provide the necessary facilities to transport it over their own routes.

I take no exception to the hon. gentleman's reference to the fact that I voted for the expenditure of money in very large amounts prior to the war. I did so, and I have no regrets for so doing. However, I stated some time ago that the financial conditions of Canada have been revolutionized in the last five years. If we wanted ten, fifteen or twenty millions of dollars before the war there was no trouble whatever to get it, and nobody suffered because Canada had the money. Hon. gentlemen will recall that we formerly had surpluses of twenty-five and thirty-five millions of dollars a year. Why the cost of the con-

stiuction of the Transcontinental down to 1914 was paid out of surpluses. We also could build grain elevators and canals whenever we so minded, there was no difficulty about it at all. I am net posing as an economist because I am fond of doing so; no man who ever occupied the position of Minister of Public Works would like to engage in building as much as I would. I would be delighted if we were able to go on and construct public works, and I have enough optimism about me to think that 1 can build fairly competently, and I should like to go on and do so. But I realize the changed condition financially which ha.', taken place in this country and that if 1 am going to be true to the pos>
9 p.m. tion which I occupy and true to my conception of what a public '.nan in Canada should do, I have got to look before I leap.
Coming to the second part of my hon. friend's remarks, I heartily agree with him. When the Welland canal is completed it seems very reasonable indeed that the big freighters should go eastward as far as they can. I do not think they can ever economically go farther than Kingston at the present time but probably it would not take a great expenditure of money in order to so deepen the channel in the St. Lawrence river, so that those vessels might proceed as far as Prescott. Some months ago I visited Kingston, where I met the Board of Trade and the municipal authorities and certainly had a very pleasant day. To-day a board of engineers, of whom an engineer of the Public Works is one, are considering this very question, and I imagine that within the next month, or two months at the outside, we will have a very comprehensive report as to what in their judgment should be done for the future development of Kingston. Not only from the railway standpoint, but from the transportation point of view, and having in mind the erection of elevators and other facilities, notwithstanding the financial obligations which we have to bear, I think that something has got to be done in order to take care of the transportation problem which will be altogether changed as soon as the Welland canal is completed. What the nature of that policy will be I cannot announce this evening, because it has not been considered by the department or the Government, and I do not make any announcement with regard to matters of policy unless they have been decided upon. However, I quite agree with my hon. friend, we must provide for the changed conditions
fttr. ('arvDll 1
in respect to transportation which will exist when the Welland canal is completed. We are thoroughly investigating the situation at Kingston, and a report will be presented inside of two months showing what the " layout " will be and the probable cost of any works that may have to be undertaken.
Mr. OOP-P: What title or interest has the Government in the property which is being improved at Toronto as a result of the channel which is being dredged through Ashbridge's bay? In consequence of the works that are in progress certain industrial sites will be created and I would like to know who will own those sites?
,Mr. (CAtRVELL: With the exception of three or four acres on the western side of the channel, the property will belong to the Toronto Harbour Commission.

We are sipending a large
amount of money on the Toronto harbour works, which will amount, when the contract is finally completed, to something like $7,000,000. I can quite understand the Public Works Department building wharves in order to improve shipping facilities, but I remember when this vote was before the House last year, or a similar appropriation, there was a good deal of discussion, and it was claimed by some members that no inconsiderable part of the money was being expended in the improvement of private property. In other words, that the property fronting on the lake was privately owned, and cellar walls were being built on that property out of the public funds-. Whether that is true or not I cannot say, but in glancing over last year's debate such is the tenor of some of the arguments that were advanced at that time. The Minister of Public Works last year explained that as a result of dredging a channel through the property in question some very valuable industrial sites would be created-indeed, some of these sites had already been built upon by business concerns, and others were in course of construction.
If that work continues and the property adjoining this channel becomes- valuable, and the Government is protecting it, I cannot see why the Government should not have some control over the disposition of it.

I thought I had already answered that question. I have stated that under the contract this property belongs to the Toronto Harbour Commission, with the exception of five or six acres. There is something in what my hon. friend says, but you must remember that every time you develop a harbour or build a wharf or pier you are

going to benefit somebody's property. The Government does not own all the property joining such improvements, and of course it would not be possible for it to do so. It is true that new property is being created by this work.
That is the point I make.

No doubt; and the property will belong to a public body-the Toronto Harbour 'Commission. I have no doubt that they will lease it, probably at some profit, although I understand that as far as the Toronto Harbour Commissioners are concerned any money they may make is for the purpose of providing extra accommodation, just the same as in the case of money that is being expended by this department. My friend referred to something about cellar walls. That is new to me; 1 do not know anything about the matter at all. I also want to say that none of this money is being expended for the protection of private property. As I explained before, it is being expended for the development of Ashbridge's bay-which I have described very fully-and for building the sea wall in front of property that has been reclaimed by the Toronto Harbour Commissioners by pumping sand out of the bottom of the lake.

My objection to this reclaiming of land is that it is too expensive. There is plenty of land in Canada, and I presume the city of Toronto could grow toward the place where the land is and. not go out into the lake for it.

If Toronto grows inland it will not have water for these industries. I want to make this as plain as I can. The idea is to provide a location for industries, and a very great number of them, that will have both rail and water transportation; and you cannot get both anywhere in Toronto that I know of except in Ashbridge's bay.

If the hon. member will satisfy this Committee that the shipping from the city of Toronto is so congested that there is no't enough water frontage at present to accommodate it, I readily agree with him that it is necessary to extend the water line. But that is the only condition of things existing in the city of Toronto or any other city that would justify the Government in building frontage at such a high cost as this must be. If this money is necessary in the sense I have suggested I would be in hearty accord with the proposed expenditure, but I am not satisfied that it
ks#
is a good business proposition to spend this money in order to give more dockage to the city unless it is absolutely necessary. That is my criticism.

I thought I had answered .that criticism once before. I have no figures before me, but in my judgment this additional water frontage is not an absolute necessity under present conditions. But I fio believe when the Welland canal is completed and the city of Toronto has access to all the Great Lakes that there will be a great many times the amount of shipping to and from that city that there is at the present time; and that was the only justification, and a complete justification, for the expenditure of this money. There is no attempt to help any private individual,, because, as I have already said, this property becomes vested in the Toronto Harbour trustees and there is no private interest involved so far as I know.	,
In view of the fact that this work is not of immediate necessity vwould it not be well to defer proceeding With it until some later date when it does become really necessary?

I am deferring it to such fin extent that some of my friends from Toronto are not altogether pleased. I am trying to finish up the harbour proposition. I believe it ought to be done, and for the present I am asking only for an appropriation to complete the sea wall in iso far as it has been started, and of course it is deteriorating all the time while in an incomplete state.
Has the Government in mind the deepening of the St. Lawrence to facilitate the passage of deep draught lake vessels to Montreal ?

That would be a pretty big question to answer. I can state this much for the benefit of my hon. friend, that a committee, composed of the engineers of some of our departments in Ottawa, the chief engineer of the Hydro Electric Commission of Ontario, and the chief engineer, I believe, of the Public Works Department of Quebec, Mr. Amos, have been working for some years on the problem of canalizing the St. Lawrence river; data has been collected, and the matter is in such shape that a report will be available in a couple of months at the outside, I would imagine. There is also a proposal, which I think will be carried out, that in a very short time this question should be handed over to the

International Joint Waterways Commission in order that they may take the data which our engineers and the American engineers may be able to give them, and investigate what the probable cost of canalizing the river would be, the amount of water-power that could be developed as the result of canalization, what it would cost to develop, what it could be sold for and where it could be sold. So I can assure my hon. friend that we are going into the matter in a thorough way, and I believe that within a year the public both of Canada and the United States will have all the information on the subject that it is possible to obtain. When that information is available, then it becomes: First, an international question; if this work is to be developed, when it is going to be developed, the expense of the development and in what proportions it should be borne, and secondly, how much money it is going to take, how much power can be developed, what is going to become of it, and how much revenue can be made out of it. I sincerely hope that it will be treated as a business proposition, and I believe that it will not be very many years before this great work is undertaken-one of the greatest in the Dominion of Canada. But we must remember that it is an international proposition to a great extent, and therefore it must be worked out between ourselves and the United States authorities. But I believe they are anxious to have it developed, if possible. I know our authorities are of the same mind, and I know we are taking every possible means to gather the fullest data for presentation to Parliament in connection with it.

Mr. C'OPP: What I have to say will not be new to the minister because I already have had some conversation with him about a public building for the city of Moncton. The building there now is very small and was erected some twenty-five years or more ago, when Moncton was only a small town. The city is growing very rapidly and has

I am sure that if the minister would have a report made on the situation he would come to the conclusion that a public building must be erected in Moncton in the very near future.
Some of us are very disappointed that no appropriation appears in the Estimates for public buildings in other parts of New Brunswick. I refer particularly to the town of Sackville in the county of Westmorland. We have never had a public building there, although we have a population of between 3,000 and 4,000 and the town is prosperous and growing rapidly. In the town of Sackville we have the Mount Allison institution, which is known all over Canada, if not all over the world, and at which a large number of students attend. I't is hardly necessary for me to impress upon the minister that a public building is very urgently needed in Sackville because he knows the locality very well. Apparently, however, the Government does not see its way clear to make an expenditure for this purpose this year. I sincerely trust that the minister will give the matter serious 'consideration and see if he cannot include an item in the Supplementary Estimates to provide for a public building in the town of Sackville. The building we are now using is one of the oldest in the town and is not much better than a common shed on a farm. It is exceedingly inconvenient for postal purposes, because the proper facilities are entirely lacking. There are hardly any boxes for the delivery of mail and people have to stand in the lobby till the mail is sorted, and sometimes, if the mail train is an

hour late, the lobby will be full and people will be standing in the cold outside, which is very unpleasant on a stormy night.

I may as well state in answer to my hon. friend the position in which I find myself in regard to public buildings all over Canada. As hon. gentlemen know, I come from the province of New Brunswick and I am very intimately acquainted with all the cities and towns of that province. I know the exact truth of everything my hon. friend (Mr. Copp) has said about the town of Sackville, but what can be said of Sackville can be said, I suppose, of fifty or a hundred towns in Canada. When I began to make up the Estimates, after four years of war, I found that promises of public buildings had been made to a great many cities and towns, and in many cases the sites had been purchased. Since the armistice, members of the House, boards of trade, and municipal bodies have told me "Now is the time to implement these promises and start the construction of these buildings." The matter was taken up by Council and considered .very carefully. I do not know whether we .were right or not, but the policy decided upon by the Government was not to construct buildings in the smaller towns and .villages at the present time; and as the Estimates show, we have provided only for ,the construction of buildings in half a .dozen of the larger centres. This was done, ,as 1 explained in the debate op the Address, partly for the purpose of providing employment in the large cities where we .knew there would be a great number of unemployed, but even in those places we are not erecting buildings if they are not required and will have no economic value.
Personally, I am a great believer in a neat small building for every town in the Dominion of Canada. It adds to the appearance of the town and gives people some *ocal pride. Furthermore, I think that the ground surrounding the building should be beautified. If there is one thing we have neglected in connection with our public buildings in the past, it is the beautifying of the grounds.
Hear, hear.

My hon. friend says, Hear hear. He and I had this very matter up a year ago, when I was trying to help him and the municipality of Three Rivers carry out this very idea. I tell the House frankly that the Iquestion of constructing public

buildings in the smaller towns is a matter of policy for the Government to decide. When the Government decides in favour of erecting these public buildings, I suppose the burden will be cast upon me of saying where the money wfll be expended, and that is not a pleasant duty, I can assure the Committee. But I must assume the responsibility when that time comes, and do the best I can. If we were back in the days of 1914, and I was Minister of Public Works, I would not hesitate to ask for an expenditure of $4,000,000 or $5,000,000 for the construction of a public building in every town in Canada with a population as low even as 1,000. Considered purely from the standpoint of dollars and cents, it would not be good business, because a building can be rented for much less than the annual interest charge and maintenance, but I think a public building in a small town has an educative value. It gives people a pride in their town, and I look upon it as a good way to spend public money.
These remarks will apply to at least fifty different constituencies in Canada and perhaps a hundred, and I thought it well to make this statement so early in the debate in order that members might know exactly the position of affairs.

Would it not be possible in connection with the erection of small buildings in towns to have a rule laid down that if the income arising from the Post Office, or the Customs, amounts to so much, that would justify the expenditure of a sum in proportion? To say that we like to see fine public buildings throughout the country is merely to say that we enjoy the beautiful. Everybody does. But we are face to face with a condition which the Minister of Public Works realizes as well as, and probably better than a great number of other people do, and I think it would hold up the minister's hands in his struggle for economy if he would lay down the rule that when an application is made for the erection of a public building in this place and the other, the income must justify the expenditure which will be involved. I would like to know what the minister has to say to that suggestion.

There is a good deal of merit in the suggestion of my hon. friend in so far as the postal revenue is concerned. I cannot agree with him as regards the Customs revenue, because in very many places in Canada the Customs revenue may be entirely out of proportion to the amount of business actually done, for the reason that

it extends to many outside points. As a rule the nearer a place to the border the greater the Customs revenue is as compared with an inland city or town. Take the town in which I live. There are only 4,000 people and we are ten miles from the border. I am not sure, but I think the Customs revenue runs close to $100,000. I am speaking from memory, but I know that it is a pretty large amount for a town of its size. That would not be a criterion as to what kind of a public building we should have because it serves a territory seventy-five miles up the river. I do not think you can take the Customs as much of a guide, but my opinion is that the postal revenue should serve to some extent as a guide as to the necessity for public buildings.

The minister has hardly answered my question as to whether it would not assist him or any Minister of Public Works in an effort to economize and to restrain the spending proclivities of the people, to lay down the rule that if the postal revenue, for instance, amounted to so much, the expenditure on a post office building should be proportionate. I know of place after place in Canada which for .several years was adequately served by a small rented building, and the total expenditure in the upkeep of the building, including rent and everything might be under a thousand dollars a year. Public buildings have been put up in these places and possibly one item such as heating may cost that much money. Of course, I am not giving exact figures; this is merely by way of illustration. I am perfectly certain that hundreds of thousands of dollars have been uselessly expended on the public services of Canada in order perhaps to meet the more or less justifiable pride of this or the other little place which demands public buildings of a character far more pretentious than the circumstances warrant.

So far as I know, the revenue is always taken into consideration. I have no figures before me, but if my hon. friend should come to the department I could show him that there is not a proposed building in Canada in connection with which we have not the data as to population, postal revenue, customs revenue, etc. We certainly consider that and take all the data into account. There are, however, some cases in which you would have to depart from that rule because you might have a pretty large population which for some reason was not contributing very much to the postal revenues. Very often a train going
through the town is the most convenient place to mail letters, and people get stamps from all sources. It is a fair criterion but it is not absolutely perfect.

I trust my hon. friend from Brome, who happens to have lived in Montreal, is not trying to excuse the expenditure on the post office in the city of Montreal because the revenues of that city were large.

My remarks upon this question of expenditure are not influenced either by the part of the country I live in, or by the part of the country I represent. I *am endeavouring as far as possible to take a Canadian view of the question. I am thoroughly convinced that very difficult financial times confront the Canadian people unless we change their mentality in regard to what they think they should get from the Government and what they should give to the Government.

The question I desire to put to the minister is rather influenced by the part of the country I come from. These are all pure maintenance items with the exception of two. Jiuilding at Grosse Isle. I am not in a position to state exactly what may be done regarding the construction of this building until I have positive instructions from the Immigration Department. This seems to be a very large sum. I am sorry I cannot do so. In a sense the Department of Public Works is only the agent of the Immigration Department for matters of this kind. Since the beginning of the war there has been practically no immigration passing through.
I would not want the minister to base his argument on the time that has elapsed from the beginning of the war. Let us take a few years before that which were very active immigration years.

I am not in a position to give the number of immigrants who pass through that building anually but I will try and get the information. It is at the extreme entrance of the great St. Lawrence river. In the summer time probably nine-tenths of the immigration coming into this country passes up the St. Lawrence river and must go through Grosse Isle. If there is one thing in my judgment that Canada has been lax in, it has been in the management of the quarantine station. I do not think we have, paid sufficient attention to the immigrants who came in here. We have not been able to give them a proper medical inspection. Men and women have been allowed into Canada who never should have been allowed in. If there is any public building that ought to be attended to immediately it is the quarantine station. We must look after the health pf these people. I admit that $400,000 seems quite

an amount to expend in adding to an existing plant. I can assure my hon. friend that if we go on with it there will not be a dollar expended more than is necessary whether the building is erected here or at Quebec. I think there is quite an opinion in the minds of some of the officials of the Immigration Department that better results would be obtained if this building were erected at Quebec.
Is this in addition to the existing building?

I come from the constituency in which the Grosse Isle plant is situated. This island is divided into two portions. There is a place provided for first class immigrants and also for the second and third class immigrants. The second and third class immigrants are using a shed that we would not think fit for cattle. The lower part of the island is specially set apart for certain diseases and the minister and the immigration authorities know tha't we had oases of bubonic plague there last summer. In that part of the island there is no proper accommodation whatever. There are a few houses but no hospital of any kind to take care of any serious cases. Millions of dollars have already been spent at Grosse Isle but no accommodation has been provided. The growing town of Montmagny, with a population of*4,000 or 5,000 is not far away and without proper accommodation at Grosse Isle diseases may spread through the town. I would impress upon the mind of the minister the desirability, as soon as possible, of erecting some part of this hospital. It would serve to improve the facilities at the quarantine station and help our part of the country by giving employment to people who were thrown out of work by the closing down of factories at the end of the war. We have a lot of unemployed men. This is a good time to build because so many people are out of work. We might here apply the argument used by the Acting Premier (Sir Thomas White) who says that we should give the people work so that the working classes will not go in for Bolshevism. I have heard that the Government has bought an island near Rimouski with the intention of removing the quarantine station there. Is that right or wrong? I am just speaking from hearsay.
I am also speaking from hearsay but I have no recollection of having heard anything about that.
I heard it and I wanted to ask the minister whether there was any truth in it.

I do not think there is anything in it. The only thing I have heard is the proposition that it might be removed to Quebec. I think the hon. gentleman is correctly describing the conditions which exist at Grosse Isle. The accommodation there is absolutely unfit for human beings, at least it is not suitable for any human beings coming to our country. If we are to maintain the plant at Grosse Isle, we must provide the necessary hospital accommodation for all classes of immigrants.
Could the minister tell us now many millions have already been (expended at Grosse Isle' for immigration purposes?
Yes, the expenditure amounts to $1,143,000.
Has the contract been awarded for the new building at Grosse Isle?
A contract was awarded last autumn for the construction of a power pi ant.
That was covered by the $30,000 vote?

Yes. The work was not proceeded with during the winter time because of the difficulty of carrying it on at that time in that portion of the province. I think the contractor was given until the first of May to commence the work. I am not sure whether the work has been actually commenced or not. If not, it will be undertaken immediately and will be carried to completion.

Last year there was a very bad storm and the wharves on both sides of the river were seriously damaged. The steamer carrying on the service between the quarantine station and the mainland has been greatly handicapped in consequence, there being practically no wharf at all on the south shore.
