Mr. 'CARVELL: It the hon. gentleman will refer to the estimates he will find that * $50,000 has been appropriated for the extension of the wharf at Grosse Isle, and $6,500 for repairing a wharf.
The $50,000 is for the lower wharf at Grosse Isle, but there are two wharves.
As I read the items we are repairing cne wharf and extending the other.

I frankly admit the soundness of everything the minister has said as to the necessity of having proper accommodation for the immigrants coming to this country by way of Grosse Isle, but that is not the point I tried to make. The point is that we are asked to pass an item of $400,000, which is a large sum of money, and the minister, whether he is acting for another department or not, should tell us why this amount is required; what accommodation has to be provided, and why we require to vote such a large sum. After all, the responsibility for the passing of these items is not merely upon the Minister of Public Works, it rests upon every member of the House, and it is a responsibility which I am afraid a number of us take very lightly. I lay it down as a matter of principle that when a minister asks us to approve of large expenditures of public moneys, every reasonable detail that we would exact if we were spending our own money should be placed before us.

I concur in practically everything which my hon. friend has said, but I have already stated that we must have proper accommodation at Grosse Isle. The immigration officers say that the work there will be proceeded with and that the expenditure of this $400,000 is imperative. I have not personally inspected the work at Grosse Isle, I am not even sure that my engineers or architects have been there. We certainly scrutinized this vote carefully, and we held it up last year because there were no immigrants coming to Canada. We did not care to expend this money while the war was in-progress, but now that it is over I look upon the equipment of our quarantine station at Grosse Isle as a prime necessity. If I had time I might go down and look over the work myself.
10 p.m. Failing that, I can only say that the reports I have received from the Immigration Department and the officers of my department, in so far as they have made any report on the matter, are that it is an absolutely necessary work. I quite admit that a $400,000 plant is quite . a plant. I have the plans and the full details before me, and they certainly indicate that if the work goes on the plant will be thoroughly up-to-date. There will be nothing in this country, or in fact on the continent, in the way of an immigration plant that will be superior to the one at the mouth of the St. Lawrence river. I do not know that I can say anything more with respect to the work. I certainly do not intend to expend any money unless

it is necessary, but I am compelled to accept the report of the officials of both departments, who say that the present accommodation is not suitable and the expenditure of this money in providing better accommodation is therefore necessary.

The disturbing
thing to my mind is the statement of an hon. member that over a million dollars has already been expended at Grosse Isle and there is absolutely no accommodation for the immigrants. It is beyond me to understand what has been done with all .that money, if that is the condition of affairs at the present time, and whether jt can be remedied or not by voting $400,000 I do not know. Surely there must be something wrong with the statement in question.

I will give my hon.
friend a statement of the money which has been spent. The expenditure up to .Confederation was $126,000, and from that time until March 31, 1918, $736,000. The balance of $180,000 is for the construction of wharves running away back to Confederation.
What have we got in return for the expenditure of that money?

I do not know, because I have not been there. We have two wharves at Grosse Isle that were pretty badly shattered during the great storm in November last. We have buildings there and a hospital and disinfecting plant, but they are out of date; they are not fit for occupation. I wish I could give my- hon. .friends more information than I have done; jf further information is desired I will endeavour to obtain it for them.

The complaint I make is not that the minister does not in a most .complete and able manner lay before us the information in his possession. My complaint is that he should have much piore information than he seems to have. He should be able to tell us, for example, whether he expects to be able to provide .accommodation, under ordinary circumstances, for so many immigrants.

If the Apostle Paul were here he could not answer that question. I do not know what the conditions are going to be in the next few years. I do not know .whether ten thousand or a million immigrants will come into Canada.

The Apostle Paul is being continuously drawn into the discussions in this House and this is not a theological seminary. If the minister has not any more idea of the number of immigrants that may be expected than he appears to have, why is he proposing to expend the sun; of $400,000 for their accommodation? Surely he must have some idea; he is' not going ahead in the dark without any definite ideas. It seems to me that he should be able to say whether or not the present equipment is inadequate. '
I have said so.

Then he should tell us that we require to have a hospital there and that it will cost about so much; that there is need for so many waiting rooms, and they will cost so much. He should give us some idea of how he proposes to lay out this $400,000, and what the necessity for it is. It is easy enough to say that he wants to make adequate preparation. We all do, but what is meant by adequate preparation?

Does it mean that all
the immigrants coming into Quebec will pass through these buildings and be detained there for examination, or does it mean that only those who are sick will go to these buildings? Which of these plans is to be followed?

As it is a quarantine
station I suppose it means only those who are sick will have to be accommodated there; but of course if there happens to be an infectious disease on the vessel the whole passenger list will have to be accommodated. There might be times when there would not be one immigrant there; there might be times when there would be a thousand. That is how I understand it, and I think that is really the condition of affairs.

I have been on a ship when we vrere -all ordered off at Grosse Isle, and I had a hard job in dodging the order myself. I can understand that for the detention of immigrants you would require a large amount of accommodation; but if only for cases of actual sickness you would not need so much accommodation. I am not complaining about the item, I only want to know what accommodation it is intended to cover.
Grosse Isle is the place where ships are held up for medical examination.

All passengers do not
land there.

I know. If a ship comes up the river with a clean bill of health she is merely stopped while the examination is taking place, and then proceeds to Montreal. But if a ship comes in with smallpox or bubonic plague on board, then the whole-list of passengers must be disembarked and taken care of at Grosse Isle.

No.

I find myself for once in full agreement with the minister. Grosse Isle station for the past few years has been in a disgraceful condition-in fact so disgraceful that it was no encouragement to immigrants. There have been times to my knowledge when four of five ships have been held up at Grosse Isle to be examined, and passengers have had to get off. Some accommodation must be found for them. You cannot run up a camp in a few minutes.
I do not know and I do not suppose the minister could tell the number of immigrants on those boats that may be accommodated in the future; but I think adequate accommodation should be provided.

When this building is completed we will be able to house all our public services in' that city.
Will this, complete it?

No, it will take $2,000,000. The work is in progress. We called for tenders simply for excavating and preparing the site for the erection of the building. I think Lyall & Son are the contractors. I do not know exactly what we will do next, but my present intention is to call for tenders for the foundation in order that no time may be lost. If we are able to have the place prepared so that we can call for tenders for the construction of the whole building and lose no time during the summer, we will do so; otherwise we will call for tenders and give a contract for the foundations, and that will give us plenty of time to complete the plans for the general structure. But the intention is to keep the work going and use as much labour as is possible in that very congested centre.
There is another item of $520,000, wh ch will complete the Government's portion of the new railway station now being erected in Toronto. Hon. members will remember that one end of that building is being constructed by the Dominion Government as a postal station.
Mr. Chairman, may I have the permission of the Committee and the minister to ask a question on the last item? What is this public building in Montreal, $500,000 ?

We skipped over that; I am sure I had no intention of doing so, but the Committee wanted to get along. That $500,000 is to build an extension to the new customs building that was erected some three or four years ago. The land was purchased, plans were prepared, and we are simply now taking up the work as we found it. There again we have called for tenders for the excavation and the foundations, and we will then proceed with the construction work on practically the same lines as I have described in respect to Toronto. In other words, we will keep men working on that building during the whole summer, and I hope it will be far enough advanced to keep them employed during the winter. It will cost probably a million and a half dollars when completed; $500,000 we figure is as much as can be economically expended during the present year.

Do we understand that these buildings, one in Montreal and

another in Toronto, are being erected chiefly to provide employment for labour rather than as being necessary for the public service?

No; I say they are necessary for the public service. We are to-day renting space in Toronto as great as that provided for in the new building, and I think probably more in the city of Montreal than we are providing for. Therefore as these works are a necessity we are constructing them under the present abnormal conditions for the purpose of providing labour for unemployed men. I have no hesitation in saying that we could get along for a year or two, because we could continue paying the rentals which we are now paying, and possibly the cost of construction will go down and money might be saved if we waited for three or four years. But I hope I have made it plain from the beginning that we feel the burden is cast upon the Government to provide as far as possible for unemployment. I am afraid we are facing a pretty serious condition from the labour standpoint. It will not be so bad during the summer months, but when the winter comes I rather shudder at the prospect. I am rather afraid there will be a great many people out of work. Therefore I think the Government should go ahead as fast as it can so long as it proceeds on economic principles and construct works that will be of economic value. As long as we can do that I think we are justified in going ahead and providing work for the unemployed.
Is there a real want of employment for men engaged in the building trades in Canada?
Yes, without a doubt.

Is it the policy of the
Government to call for tenders for all public works?

Yes, even in connection with' the foundations; and invariably we accept the lowest tender. The difference between the highest and lowest tenders in some cases would surprise hon. gentlemen. In the case of the Toronto building the lowest tender was $17,000 or $18,000 and the highest was over $40,000. By calling for tenders in this way we can start work immediately on the first part of the building, and by the time the foundation is completed we have the plans and specifications ready for the whole structure. On the other hand, we may have the plans ready in time to call for tenders for the

construction of the whole building, including the foundation.

In speaking of the
foundation, does the minister mean both the excavation and the concrete foundation?
The contracts now running are for the excavation. We may call for tenders subsequently for the concrete foundations, to be built to the ground line or perhaps two or three feet above the ground line.

What is the excavation costing per cubic yard? The only way of telling whether the work is being done at a reasonable rate is by knowing the quantity that has to be removed and the cost of removing it.

Before calling for tenders a very careful estimate is prepared by officials of the department, and hon. gentlemen would be surprised to see how close the lowest tenders usually come to the official estimate. Up to the middle of last summer, when prices were going up all the time, the tenders usually ran above the departmental estimate, but during the last six months the tenders have been below the departmental estimate in the great majority of cases. In the case of the Toronto works the tender is a little below the departmental estimate.

Is any principle laid down by the Government with regard to the class of labour employed in the construction of these buildings? People who are not citizens of Canada, who have not taken out naturalization papers, who are foreigners, should not be employed in these public works. The work should be given to -Canadian citizens, especially to returned soldiers. That principle should be laid down by the Government so that the contractor will know the class of labour that he must employ.
Mr. C'ARVELL: We have not begun to lay down, when calling for tenders, the class of labour that must be employed. But we have had a chance now of studying the matter closely, and we find that returned soldiers are not willing to dig trenches; they dug all the trenches they wanted to in Prance. There is no disguising the fact that the returned -soldier does not want to engage in such labour as the preparing of foundations.

I agree.
Mr. 'CARVELE: I do- not know to what extent foreign labour is employed in this
particular class of work, but I think there would be some difficulty in getting ordinary Canadians to go into the ground and help take out the foundation for a building. If the time should come when it would -be necessary to exclude foreigners from work on the construction of these buildings, I would not hesitate to do -so, but we have not reached that point yet. There is not such an abundance of that class of labour in Canada at the present time that we would be justified in drawing the line.

With regard to the Quebec Marine Department stores, what steps is the minister going to take to call for tenders? The building is an eyesore in its present condition, situated, as it is, directly under the terrace at Quebec. I hope the minister will do his utmost to have this work finished as rapidly as possible. I understand that more than a month must elapse in connection- with calling for tenders, and this delay will bring us into November. If the minister can go on with this work at once he will be doing justice to the city of Quebec and to his department.
Mr. -ClARVELL: I imagine that the plans and specifications are already -prepared. When the percentage of the Estimates was voted two or three weeks ago I instructed the proper officials not to wait for the passing of the main Estimates, but to get out the plans and specifications and call for tenders. Tenders for a great many works are -being called at the present time, even before the money is voted. I realize the importance of starting this work as early in the summer as possible. There should be no difficulty in having it finished before next November. I assure my hon. friend that it will be attended to before the cold weather comes.
Mr. MoMASTER: It may not be altogether desirable to spend too much money on building or excavating when such a tremendous need for agricultural labour exists throughout the country. Speaking for my part of the province of Quebec, I may say that farmers are complaining very bitterly of their inability to get farm labour. I know that it would be a very difficult thing to do, but if it is at all possible I suggest that currents of labour be deflected from the towns to the country, where labour is very much needed and where, under present conditions, it is not inadequately remunerative.
Mr. -CARVELL: That is a very pious suggestion. Perhaps my hon. friend will point out some way of accomplishing it.

Mr. MdMASTER: I suggest that in connection with the housing scheme the Government proposes to bring down, some money might very properly be spent in assisting farmers, at a low rate of interest, to put up labourers' cottages in the country. That would help very substantially to get farm labour on the land.

The minister a few moments ago said that one of the objects in going on with public works in different places was to give employment to the idle. If there are so many idle people in Canada that we have to make spechil provision for them like this, at a time when the cost of labour and material is so expensive, I do not see how the minister can ask for $400,000 for the erection of an immigration building. Surely, if there are so many idle people in Canada we should not have immigrants coming in. Some weeks ago the minister was deploring the financial condition of the country and wondering how we were going to meet our obligations, but judging by the Estimates he seems to have forgotten his fears on that score. I admit that we must keep abreast of the times and put up buildings where they are actually needed, but I do not think it is good business to go on. erecting public buildings for the sake of giving work to the unemployed and at the same time encourage immigration to this country.
Would my hon. friend name one item that he would like to see deleted?

Yes; all the items on the list. The minister is asking for three times as much as he did last year. He is asking for money to construct new buildings and to repair old ones. Perhaps I should not complain, because I am producing and selling the materials used in construction, but it certainly is an expensive time to engage in construction work. I think the item for the immigration building should stand.
I notice that a rural mail shelter is to be provided at Walker-ton. Is this a new departure for the Government to provide rural mail shelters and what is the nature of the shelter?

It is only a shed for the protection of the horses of the mail carriers at the Walkerton public building. There are a number of places in Canada where this protection is provided for the carriers of rural mail.
Why is it more necessary to have a shelter at Walkerton than at other places in Ontario?

Wherever my hon friend finds an item of this kind, it has been requested by the Post Office Department.
Alberta-public works chargeable to income-[DOT] $5'32,0'0'0.
Will the minister explain this item?

This amount is required for the erection of a general public building in Calgary. My hon. friend, I think, is acquainted with that part of the country and knows that the only post office accommodation they have in Calgary is in a wooden shack, which they have been occupying for four or five years. We have been compelled to rent space in the Lancaster block for two or three years. Now we are starting the construction of a public building, not a post office building, but a building that will be used by the post office and all other branches of the public service in the city of Calgary. I am absolutely opposed to the erection of a public building simply for the use of the post office or the custom house or anything of that kind. I find that once you hand oveT a building to tlie^ post office, you can never get anything else into it, and when it comes to the custom house, it is as easy for a camel to go through the eye of a needle as it is get other branches of the public service in there. I like to call them public buildings, so that they will be open to all officials of the public service in these cities.
Is this a new building?

Yes. It will cost $780,000 when completed.
, Mr. FIELDING: You are calling it a post office building.
It will be used by the post office.
According to my hon. friend's statement, if the post office gets in there, nobody else will be able to get into it.
We will set apart a certain amount of space for the post office.
And they will appeal to the vote when you try to get anybody else in there.
Has the contract been let for this building, and if so, to whom?
No, but we shall be ready to call for tenders for the excavation almost immediately. I imagine we will carry out the same policy there that we did in Montreal and Toronto.

This policy of excavating the foundation has resulted, in Montreal at least, in having the foundation, which has cost tens or hundreds of thousands of dollars, remain without any superstructure upon it for several years, and the loss of interest through dead capital must have run into very large figures. I mention this merely by way of warning, but of course it may not be necessary with the present minister.
I am quite well aware of it, and I am also aware that there has been quite a war on since those foundations were put in.
We are reminded that there has been a war on altogether too often. That is no excuse for poor business. The war cannot be dragged in as an excuse for something that is otherwise inexcusable.
The war was a good reason for delaying construction.
The taunt about there having been a war on is thrown across this floor altogether too often, and I do not propose to continue to bear it with that equanimity which usually characterizes my conduct.

There is an item of $400,000 for Calgary and $100,000 for Edmonton, and the total is $532,000 on public buildings in Alberta. The population of Alberta is not as large as that of Saskatchewan, and the buildings in Saskatchewan are not any better than those in Alberta. I do not quite understand why we should have to spend over $500,000 on public buildings in Alberta when it is only necessary to spend $38,000 in Saskatchewan. I know that Saskatoon, Regina, and Moosejaw are no better equipped at present than Edmonton. Calgary has only a temporary building, and it seems an unusual thing that Alberta should have over $500,000 and Saskatchewan practically nothing when they require the buildings just as much. If the minister is spending the money in order to provide employment, I think there should be just as much need in one province as in the other.

I hope my friend does not entertain the idea that I am trying to
spend. money territorially. I do not purpose to spend a dollar anywhere unless it is necessary, if I can help it. It happens that they do not require public buildings in the large cities of Saskatchewan; they are well supplied, and as I have been in them all I know just as much about the question as does my hon. friend. There are many smaller towns in Saskatchewan where public buildings are needed, and I wish it were possible to grant them. I have explained the situation as regards that class of public buildings. It happens that in Alberta a different condition exists. There is no place for the post office, and there is no post office at all. As regards Edmonton, I was in that city last autumn and went through all the public buildings, and the congestion is serious. We have officials housed in half a dozen different places, and we must be paying, roughly speaking, $35,000 to $40,000 a year in rentals in the city of Edmonton. Something must be done to meet the situation. I have asked for a vote of $100,000. I am not sure that we are justified in erecting buildings. I think we could purchase a building in the city of Edmonton that would meet all the requirements and one that would be cheaper and very much better than any we could construct. I do not know, however, that we would be justified in spending money for the purchase of buildings to-day when we think it is our duty to spend it in such a way as will provide labour for employment. That is the difficulty that exists. I am very much at a loss to know what to do in the city of Edmonton. If I followed my own inclinations and viewed the question as a business proposition, there are two" or three buildings I could buy at a great discount on what they cost, and probably for 50 per cent of what we could erect a building for.
Why not purchase then?
I have not said we are not going to. We will consider the matter carefully.

I understand it is the policy of the department to construct buildings wherever they are needed rather than to purchase, in order to give employment to those who are out of work, no matter whether the buildings will cost twice what they would if they were purchased. Is that a good business policy? Is this Government being run on business principles or as an eleemosynary institution?

I do not think my friend is justified in such an inference. I have



not said that I purpose to construct buildings that will cost twice as much as if existing buildings were purchased. I have said that in some places-and have given the details-we will construct buildings because they are necessary. We believe they will cost more than in ordinary times, but we believe that it is necessary to provide work, in addition to the fact that the buildings are required. When we come to Edmonton, the situation is a little different from some of the other places. I do not know that there is the same necessity for employment there as elsewhere, and I am considering seriously whether we would not be justified in exercising the strictest business principles in purchasing rather than building. The matter is absolutely open and will have to be decided as one of policy before we are able to act one way or the other. We must come to a decision before Parliament prorogues.
This sum now asked for is for the purpose of purchasing.
No, it is for building.
The question of purchasing will-not be taken into account?

No, unless we decide as a matter of policy to purchase, in which case we must come back for a supplementary estimate to get the money voted.
Mr, JACOBS: As I understand it, the cost of purchasing will be about half, so that it will not be necessary to have supplementary estimates.
Mr. CARVELL; You cannot buy a build' ing in Edmonton that will be suitable to house the public services there for $50,000 nor $100,000. This is for an addition to the present post office building. If we decide as a matter of policy that we will purchase a building we will not require this money, and this vote will lapse, but we will have to come back to Parliament, set forth the facts, and have the money for purchase voted.
Is not this the proper time to tell us what the policy of the Government is with respect to the construction or the purchase of public buildings?

I have not had the opportunity of discussing this question with my colleagues and I cannot make a statement until I am authorized to do so. I have intimated to the Committee my views on the matter. I think there is a very grave question whether we should not purchase in Edmonton rather than build hut nothing 
will be done until Parliament is apprised of it. If we decide to purchase we must come to Parliament.

Would it not be well to
hold this item until the Government makes up its mind?

I do not think there
would be much use in doing that. If we do not purchase we must provide additional accommodation and this vote is for the purpose of providing that accommodation. If we do not require it we shall not use it.

Do the rentals that are
being paid now in Calgary and Edmonton amount to much more than the interest on the capital invested in a new building?

I am not in a position
to give the exact details. Speaking from memory I think we pay $35,000 or $40,000 a year for rentals in both Calgary and Edmonton. I shall be glad to bring the exact figures before the Committee. There is no secret about it. I am sure we are paying as much in rentals now as we would pay in interest on a new building in each one of the cities and every hon. gentleman must see a great advantage in having all the officials of the Government housed in one building with one janitor service and one control rather than have them scattered over a half dozen different places in each city.

I hope the minister will go. into this matter of public buildings in Edmonton very carefully. I heard with a good deal of pleasure his statement as to the possible policy of the department in connection with public buildings, particularly in Edmonton. The services of the Government in Edmonton are scattered over the entire city and from the point of view of the convenience of the public there the arrangement is a bad one. The rental the Government is paying in Edmonton for publie service would pay the interest on a million dollar building, and the Government would be well advised to go into the question and consider whether it would not be advisable to buy a building and have the services all under one roof than to build under existing conditions.
The commission travelling throughout the West now report there is little unemployment in Calgary and Edmonton. Would it not be advisable to leave the Calgary building for another year?

I cannot agree with the suggestion of my hon. friend. I think we ought to go on with the construction of a

public building in Calgary. This work is of such importance as to demand that we shall proceed with it.

There are two grounds which the minister could well take for the construction of this building and he has taken both. One is the public necessity for the use of the building, and the other is building in order to give employment for those who are looking for work. My hon. friend (Mr. Cahill) suggests that he is informed there is not much unemployment in the west. A couple of days ago I met a very distinguished westerner, an officer of the Grain Growers' Association, my good friend, Mr. Roderick McKenzie, a well known public character in the west, and he told me it was extremely difficult to get help. I asked him if the farmers were going to get their work done this spring and he said it was extremely difficult to get help on the farm. I do not think any man who can get work on the farm should be the subject of any worry to the Government with regard to providing -work for him. We find a gieat many of our young men in the east willing to go out and work on the farm in what is known as harvesting and I suppose spring work, planting and seeding are not any harder than harvesting. If thousands of our young men used to be able to go out in the -west in harvesting time and be serviceable at that season, I do not see why men, rather than being allowed to remain idle, should not be encouraged to go and work on the farm and be of use to the country generally. The minister said that he did not know of any means by which a man could be diverted from idleness in the towns to work on the farm. One good way would be to let them feel the necessity of getting work for themselves and employing their own energies for their own benefit. When I was a young man I had to look for work. I had no Government providing work for me; I had to go and look for it, to get it and then to go to work. I am afraid there is such a thing as too much solicitude on the part of public bodies to-day thus depriving many people of their own initiative and individuality in getting along. I think there is danger in that direction. No person will exert himself to provide for himself if he thinks the Government is going to do everything for him and there is nothing for him to do but to sit down and say there is no work. I do not think that is what our people are looking for. They are looking for a place where they can get work. I think they are willing to do it. If there
152*
is plenty of work on the farms of Alberta,. Saskatchewan and Manitoba, I do not think we should be erecting public buildings, building railways, or undertaking any public work, for the mere purpose of giving these men work, if they can get on the	farm where	their
work will be far more productive than it would be in putting up a public building or building a railway. Of course, the building of a railway for the necessities of transportation is another matter. Rather than enter upon any public work for the mere purpose of giving.people employment and putting money in their way, I think it would be well to encourage them to go to work on the farm. If conditions in the West to-day are as they are reported to me, and as the evidence seems to indicate before the Government commission that is now going through the West, there does not seem to be very much necessity for the minister to spend money in order to provide employment.

With regard to this appropriation for a post office in Calgary, the minister has rightly stated that the building now used is a shack. It is a very ordinary shack at that. It is even worthy to be called a shanty. It is the kind of building that is used in Eastern Canada as a woodshed. If that condition existed in any eastern town, or in the Maritime-Provinces, we would soon hear about it. Why should Calgary be discriminated against in this way? Calgary is a city of about 60,000 population and yet an ordinary woodshed is being used for the purpose of the post office.

I am sorry to hear that there is any difference of opinion whatever in regard to this building in Calgary. Arrangements were made for the erection of a new post office in 1914. The old building there was burned down with the result that the city was left without any building for the post office purposes. They had to occupy temporary quarters and when those temporary quarters became absolutely unfit for human habitation they moved into other temporary quarters where they are at present and which are crowded and unsuitable. There was trouble there in connection with the employees. They were very patient up to the time that they were removed to their present quarters. The work is distributed over the city and if there is any place in Canada where a post office is needed it is Calgary. It is one of the largest postal centres in the Dominion. A building is to be erected which will be

capable of being used for purposes other than those of the post office. The Government is absolutely justified in appropriating money for this work and I only hope that the 'Department of Public Works will proceed with the erection of the building as fast as they possibly can.
British Columbia/-(public buildings, $111,475.60.

I notice one small item
for taxes on a Government building in British Columbia. I do not notice an item of this kind in any of the other provinces. I would like to know why it is the Government pay taxes on a public building in Victoria and not in other municipalities?

This is an old post office building that has been abandoned. It is a public building but a new building was erected and this is now being rented. The policy has been adopted all over Canada that when the Government ceases to occupy a building, rents it and receives a rental, it should pay taxes to the municipality. This is a small item for the purpose of paying the taxes and as against it we receive a revenue.
Are there no other public buildings throughout the Dominion of the same class?

Certainly, there are some in Ottawa. There are buildings on Wellington street in this city, in what we call the expropriated area, that are owned by the Government but are rented to other people. We receive a revenue from those buildings, and as a consequence we pay the taxes upon that particular property to the municipality of Ottawa, and we would do so under like circumstances anywhere.
There is no item in the Public Accounts to show that.
I do not know as to that. However, the facts are as I have stated.
Would the minister say what the revenue from this property in Victoria is?
I could not give the information offhand.
I want to see if we are making any money.
We are not liable to make much money on an old public building.

I do not quite see the force of the minister's philosophy in re-

gard to this renting business. If he uses the building as a post office he gets a great deal more money from the use of it than he would if a person occupied it as a tenant. If the minister is getting $10,000 for the use of a building as a post office, he would not pay any taxes, but he does if some private individual leases the property and pays $100 rent. I do not see the force of that argument.

The policy may not be based on or be good logic, but it is one with which the present Minister of Public Works is very much in love. My hon. friend knows that under the terms of the British North America Act, the Government is not subject to the payment of taxes upon any of its property; and in every city and town in Canada in which public buildings have been constructed very valuable property is therefore withdrawn from taxation by the municipality. Sometimes I wonder if it would not be better to amend the British North America Act so that the Government would pay taxes to the municipality in which its property was situated the same as any other property owner does. However, it is not necessary for me to express an opinion upon the point, because it is not an issue to-day. At the same time I have a very strong feeling in regard to this matter, and the moment the Government acquires a piece of property*which it is not occupying for Government purposes but is renting to some other person who pays a rental, I think we are bound to comply with all the municipal regulations, even as to the payment of taxes. There may not be any legal justification for that, but to me it certainly seems only fair and just to the municipality concerned.

I think that the position taken by the minister with regard to a case of the kind he mentions is right and proper, but I would like to know why this item in regard to the public buildings in British Columbia is treated very differently in the matter of book keeping from the buildings in Ottawa?

I can only say that it is a system which has been followed for some time. In the case of Ottawa the buildings were only purchased three or four years ago, but we are paying taxes just the same, and I shall be only too happy to bring down all the details. If the hon. gentleman will refer to item 120, which is set forth at page 72 of the Estimates, he

will find the designation there " Dominion Public Buildings Generally." Now we are paying the taxes on this Ottawa property and other properties throughout the Dominion out of that vote.
I think as a matter of book keeping the item should be designated in the same way as respects all Government buildings.

My hon. friend may be right, I think perhaps he is, 'out I will only be too happy to furnish all. the details required. We are Certainly paying taxes to the city of Ottawa on those buildings which we own and are renting to private individuals.

I say at once to the minister that he should stop paying taxes; the Crown is not called upon to pay them under the law. The Crown, or the Government, owns property in every part of Canada, and I think in every part of the Empire, which is exempt from taxation. Why should we make any sympathetic arrangement which is applicable to any one part of the country more than to another? There is no law for that, and it should not be done. The law provides that the property of the King shall be exempt from taxation, therefore, the minister in paying taxes on such property is paying that money out without any authority.

So far as I am concerned, it is not a question of sympathy; it is absolutely a matter of cold justice as I view it. There may possibly be some question as to whether we have a right to pay these taxes under the British North America Act. All I can read into that Act is that we are not compelled to pay taxes; but if we have a piece of property in a municipality which we are renting and receiving a revenue from I cannot see how the hon. gentleman can argue 'that we are not compelled to pay the municipal taxes upon it.
What becomes of the rent?
It goes into the consolidated revenue of the country, of course.
You do not pay the taxes with it?

No, the money goes into the consolidated revenue and we pay it out in the ordinary way.
There is another thing which I think I must tell my hon. friend: All over the country for years the Dominion Government has
been paying to municipalities local improvement taxes. If there is a street, or a sidewalk, being constructed in front of, or alongside Government property, we pay our proper share of the cost of that work, just the same as any ordinary property owner does, and we ought to do so. We owe that duty to the municipalities. I think we are just as much called upon to pay the taxes on a property from which we are receiving revenue, as we are to pay the special taxes for local ^improvement.
Does the minister not think we are entitled to know the amount of rent we are receiving?
I shall be only too happy to furnish to my hon. friend to-morrow, or whenever he wants it, all possible information.

There is another feature in connection with this vote as to which I would like to make inquiry. I have noticed in the press recently that the Mayor of Ottawa has been expressing dissatisfaction with the annual grant made by the Dominion Government towards the taxation of this city-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: If the hon. member will only wait until we reach the votes for Ottawa public buildings he will be in order in raising the point. Ottawa is very far from British Columbia.
I understand that, and I am only referring to the matter generally in connection with this item.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. gentleman had better wait until we reach the next item.

I think the Minister of Public Works is absolutely justified in the stand which he has taken. Let us assume for a moment that the Dominion Government has two or three buildings in any city in Canada which it rents out and receive revenue from. If it fails to pay its share of the taxes that burden is distributed over the other local taxpayers. So long as the Federal Govern-11 p.m. ment owns property which it is using for Government purposes, and is receiving no revenue from, the principle of tax exemption applies and should apply. But there is no reason why this Government should acquire property in any municipality and, in competition with other property owners, derive a revenue therefrom, and not assume its fair

share of taxation. I think that is absolutely unjustified.
Mr. McKENZIE .[DOT] The law, as was pointed out some 'time ago by the hon. member for Shelburne and Queens (Mr. Fielding), may be an ass, but the law nevertheless is that the King does not pay taxes. If the hon. member for Calgary (Mr. Tweedie) finds fault with the law it would be better to change it, and enact that the King, or the Government representing the King, shall pay~4axes on Government property wherever it is. But while it is the law that the King does not pay taxes, we are not called upon to make such payment. It is preferable to adhere to that law rather than to sidetrack it and from sympathetic ideas, or any notions we may have, pay taxes on a piece of property the moment we receive any revenue from it. The idea of local taxation is that a man gets his children educated, enjoys the benefit of street lighting, police protection, and all the advantages of the machinery of local government in the place where he lives; consequently he pays taxes. If he does not live in the town where his property is located, but in some other place, he should contribute to that general fund which extends to him the general benefit and protection of municipal and provincial institutions. But the King does not enjoy any of these benefits from property and therefore he does not pay any taxes. The King nominally holds this property. At all events, that is the reason why he does not pay taxes', because he does not in those various places enjoy those benefits which come from local taxation. And while it is the law that Government property is not subject to taxation it is better that we stand by the law.
I understand that Government property is not liable for general taxes; but for local improvement rates, such as a sidewalk along Government property, I think the Government should pay its share.
It is not liable.
We do pay it any way.

Discussing this item 119, I would like to call attention to the fact that there is a payment of taxes due the city of Victoria for 1918 amounting to $1,475.60. I inquired as to why this item was there and why a similar item was not in the Estimates for the other provinces, and the minister said that certain Government buildings in the city of Ottawa were paying

taxes. The question I wanted to ask before was: What amount of taxes the Government is paying?

speechtext:
I ruled that question out of order a moment ago, and I hope the hon. gentleman will abide by my ruling.
Public buildings-Generally-$185,000.

Mr. Chairman, I see
in connection with this item a charge of $5,000 for flags for Dominion public buildings, and I would like to make a few observations thereon. First of all, I would draw the attention of the Minister of Public Works to the fact that a great number- perhaps I should say most of those who are concerned in the caretaking of public buildings seem to take very poor care of the flags, and you will find the flags left up in all sorts of weather and flying by night as by day. I think this, is a matter which should be brought to the attention of those who are in charge of our public buildings: first, on the ground of economy; second, on the ground of showing an example of thrift to the people; and, third, out of respect for the flag itself.
Now, there is another matter I wish to bring before the 'Committee, and I think it may properly be brought forward in connection with this item. We have a national flag for marine purposes. Our merchant marine flies the Canadian flag; our navy flies the British ensign on one mast and the Canadian marine ensign on the other.
They were made to take it down.

I did not know that. But my submission to the Committee is that we should have a national flag for land purposes. The great Commonwealth of Australia has a national flag; I think the Commonwealth of New Zealand has a national flag, and it seems to me that the Dominion of Canada also should have a national flag. I think it would help to create a national spirit, and I believe that in the creation of a sound and sane national spirit lies the cure for many of the racial and religious troubles which are a curse to the Canadian people. The matter has received some attention in the press. I remember reading in the Montreal Weekly Witness a poem by a young lady about the necessity and desirability of a national flag. I would recommend the matter to the patriotism of the Minister of Public Works, who is apparently in charge of the flag department. I would like to see a strong and sound national spirit arise in Canada as

characteristic as the flavour of our maple syrup, and I think the matter deserves public attention. Our soldiers who fought across the seas so gallantly were proud not only of being British soldiers, but they were proud of being Canadian soldiers. As we are proud to belong to what I prefer to call the Associated British Commonwealths rather than the British Empire, I would like to see our national flag, a national flag for land .purposes, floating over our public buildings.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
In order that I may not have to call any hon. member of the Committee to order, I must point out that the discussion of the adoption of a national flag is certainly not open on the item before the House at the present time, which item is for the purchase of flags for public buildings. It may be very well, and I expected that was the idea of my good friend from Brome, to discuss what kind of flag will be purchased, whether a British flag, a Canadian flag, or a marine flag; but it is certainly not within the power of the Minister of Public Works to make a new flag for Canada at the present time. Therefore it is not in order to discuss the adoption of a national flag on this item.
Mr. CARVELL; I realize that my hon. friend from Brome has brought up a very important subject. I do not propose to answer him as to the kind of flag we are going to purchase; I think that is a matter that somebody else must decide. I quite agree with him that these flags should be taken care of, and I do think for the last three or four years there has not been the amount of care exercised that should have been. The instructions we send out from the department to the caretakers is that the flags shall be put up in the morning and be taken down at sunset, which is a proper and sensible custom. But I am afraid that during the war people wanted the flag up after those hours, and in many cases it was easier for the caretaker from his standpoint to leave the flag up all the time rather than take it down and put it up again.

Without dissenting from the view of the hon. member from Brome- that is a general question-may I ask the minister what flag is distributed officially for use on the public buildings? The reason I ask the question is that we are using improperly everywhere in Canada a red ensign, which is the flag of the Canadian merchant marine. It is not a land flag, but it is very widely used throughout
Canada at any public function; in fact, you will see one-half or more of the flags displayed for decorative purposes will be the British red ensign with the arms of Canada in the corner. That is distinctly a sea flag and is properly used by all our Canadian merchant marine. The British red ensign is the flag of the British merchant marine; the British red ensign with the arms of Canada in the corner is the flag of the Canadian merchant marine; but neither flag is a proper land flag, and yet there is an almost universal use in Canada of the red ensign with the arms of Canada in the corner. Hence I ask the question of my hon. friend, whether that flag is distributed, or whether only the Union Jack is distributed ?
We distribute only the Union Jack.
That is correct?
Yes.
I want to inquire of the minister if he has a memorandum before him as to what improvements he is going to make in the experimental farms in connection with the item of $150,000.

Yes. The item I have is " Central Farm, Ottawa, $35,000." Then are given all the details; for instance, animal husbandry, $16,000; bees, $300; botany, $3,000; cereals, $300, and so on. Then we have branch farms and stations. Tobacco curing stations, $3,525; Charlottetown, P.E.I., $10,510; Kentville, N.S., $3,500; Nappan, N.S., $5,425; Fredericton, N.B., $2,900; Ste. Anne de la Pocatiere, Que., $4,450; Cap Rouge, Que., $4,000; Lennoxville, Que., $5,650; Morden, Man., $7,300; Brandon, Man., $3,600; Indian Head, Sask., $2,000; Rosthern, Sask., $3,800; Scott, Sask., $3,450; Lethbridge, Alta., $16,175; Lacombe, Alta., $4,650; Summerland, B.C., $20,200; Invermere, B.C.,	$4,550; Agassiz, B.C.,
$5,200; Sydney, B.C., $3,300.

I want to protest, as I protested every session that I have been here, against the throwing away of money on these experimental farms. The Central Experimental Farm is a very delightful place to go to for a picnic, but particularly at this time we should not be spending money on a place for picnic purposes. Nobody likes to go there better than I do; I like looking at the things to be seen there. But it is high time that some better method was adopted to encourage agriculture. The farmers do not get any practical benefit

from these experimental farms. They are kept as picnic grounds, and to supply certain individuals with hothouse stuff-which is all very nice, but produces no revenue for the country. I simply wish to register my protest against the maintenance of these experimental farms.
Is there any amount in the Estimates to provide for an experimental farm station at Baie St. Paul in Charlevoix county?

No. We are simply the agent of the Agriculture Department in connection with the construction of these buildings, and I can only answer for what is placed before me. As to the remarks of my hon. friend (Mr. Copp), I have criticised in days gone by some of the expenditures in connection with these farms. I could pick out some of them with regard to which I have very strong views. But I cannot agree with my hon. friend's remarks in regard to the Central Experimental Farm. I realize that the farmer cannot reproduce what he sees there, because he has not the financial means. But the object of the experimental farm is not so much to show farmers how to carry on their work as to make experiments which may be valuable to any man who wishes to learn. I myself go to the experimental farm very frequently for information, and have always been able to get it. I am sorry that the people do not read and digest as thoroughly as they should the reams of information that are sent out annually from that farm as a result of the experiments that are carried on.
Could not my hon. friend get the information he desires if the farm were not there?
No, they must make the experiments in order to get the information. Theoretical information is no good to the farmer; he must have information that is based on actual experience.

I have no doubt that every member of the House received to-day a circular from the Agriculture Department containing a photograph of a corn crop that a grub was destroying. I am not much of a farmer, but I know all about the matter dealt with in this circular, as does every farmer in our part of the country. If that is what we are paying for at the experimental farm-it costs something to print these things and send them out to members of Parliament and to farmers throughout the country-we are getting mighty little for our money.

I am surprised at the expression of opinion which comes from the East in regard to the experimental farms. We in the West appreciate the benefit that is derived from the farms in the West as well as from the Central Experimental Farm at Ottawa. I point out the great benefit that has come to the country through the development of Marquis wheat, a variety developed by Dr. Saunders, which has been worth millions of dollars to Canada.

A few years ago there was a by-election in Dorchester county in which a member of the then Borden Government, Mr. Sevigny, a Cabinet minister, was a candidate and was elected by a substantial majority. This gentleman made a formal promise to the electors of that county that if he was elected an experimental farm would be established there. No experimental farm, however, has been established in Dorchester county, and I have received several letters from my electors asking that an experimental farm be established there. I see no difference between this Government and the former Government; therefor I say that the Minister of Public Works is bound by the promises that were made a couple pf years ago by a member of the Borden Cabinet. Dorchester is an ideal spot for an experimental farm. It is quite close to the city of Quebec and is in the neighbourhood of the constituency of Beauce, represented by my distinguished friend (Mr. Beland) and I think it would be beneficial to the public generally if a farm was established there. The member for Westmorland (Mr. Copp) says that in many cases the expenditure on experimental farms is a waste of money. I think it would not be a waste of money if a farm was established in my county. It was promised by a member of the Cabinet, and I think that a promise made by a minister of a government which is not different from the present one ought to be redeemed. I would suggest that if no provision has been made in the Main Estimates for this farm, the minister should provide an item in the Supplementaries, because he surely will agree that a promise should be kept.

I do not find any such item in these Estimates, but of course I am merely acting as the agent of the Minister of Agriculture, and I do not know why it has not been included. I have a recollection, however, that according to a Return brought down in this House some two years ago the then government distributed a large quantity of very valuable thorough-

bred animals throughout the county of Dorchester, but the people appreciated them so little that they at once proceeded to convert them into benevolent neutrals, and I think the department came to the conclusion that the people of the county of Dorchester really did not appreciate them. If I were called upon to give a reason, I would say that that is the reason why the minister has not included an item in the present Estimates for such a farm.

This promise of an experimental farm which was made to the electors of Dorchester by a former minister has not been carried out, but I understand that the promise was made by a minister of the preceding Government, and not of the Government of which the Minister of Public Works is a member. In view of the fact that a good deal of money was spent in the county of Dorchester during that famous election, and the fact that the county of Beauce is contiguous to the county of Dorchester, that no money was spent in the county of Beauce either during the last election or the previous one, that the county of Beauce, which was at one time mostly a timbering region has of late years been converted into a most successful agricultural district, and the further fact that Beauce county has within its borders the richest maple bushes in the whole Dominion of Canada, with an average yearly crop of some million and a half pounds of maple sugar-in view of all these considerations I really think that the county of Beauce would be an ideal spot for the establishment of an experimental farm. I do not in the least wish to convey the impression that the county of Dorchester is not a rich and fertile county, but it cannot possibly compare with the county of Beauce. The county of Beauce is one of the richest counties in the whole Dominion, both from an agricultural standpoint and in some other respects. It is ideally situated. The county of Compton, the fame of which has gone far beyond the limits of the province of Quebec, the county of Megantic, also of great repute, and the counties of Levis, Montmagny, Bellechasse and L'lslet form around the county of Beauce, as it were, a crown, and I would strongly urge the minister to impress upon his colleague the Minister of Agriculture the real urgency of establishing an experimental farm in Beauce county. It has the best location in the whole province of Quebec, and it is the best riding by far. One has only to think of the maple bushes of the county of Beauce, of its dairying, of its lumbering,
and of its cereal cultivation, to come to the conclusion that no other part of the Dominion of Canada can begin to compare with my county.
I shall be very glad indeed to convey to the Minister of Agriculture the beauties and necessities of the county of Beauce.

I am afraid the hon. member for Beauce has not travelled very extensively through the county of Renfrew or he would have a different opinion of the merits of his own county. How much taxation has been paid by the Government to the city of Ottawa on properties owned by the Government and rented out?

I am sorry I cannot give that information to-night, but I shall be very glad to bring it down, and my hon. friend need not trouble to put a question on the Order Paper. There are a number of places in Ottawa on which we pay taxes.
I have a few figures here of the taxes we pay outside of Ottawa: Bowman, $64.60; Estevan, $46.83; Ingersoll, $223.72; Montreal postal station B, $74.79; postal station H, $126.24; postal station S, $100.85.
These are taxes on buildings owned by the Government and rented?
I presume so. We pay these taxes in those places.

There is an item here of $30,000 for "Dominion public buildings-generally." I would think this item unecessary, because we have already provided for Dominion public buildings in all the provinces. Item No. 113, for instance, provides for Dominion public buildings, improvements, repairs, etc., in the Maritime provinces generally, $25,000. We have voted for Quebec, $35,000; Ontario, $35,000; Manitoba, $18,000; Saskatchewan, $15,000; Alberta, $3,000; British Columbia, $17,000. So as we have passed a general vote for repairs and improvements to public buildings in every province in Canada,. I think we might dispense with the item of $30,000 for Dominion public buildings generally.

My friend is an old enough parliamentarian to realize that it is almost humanly impossible to provide for every emergency that may arise. There may be a storm or fire and it has always been the custom to include these small amounts for emergencies. So long as I have been in Parliament these amounts

have been voted and I think they are necessary. There might be a fire or some accident and you would be absolutely tied up because the Auditor General would not pass the account unless there was some item from which it could be drawn. There is no sinister motive in this. It is only carrying out a custom of long standing and one that is absolutely necessary. Last year a building was burnt down on Partridge Island in St. John and something had to be done. There is a vote in the Estimates now, but we were called upon at once to put up something in the way of a temporary building. I do not think there is any room for genuine criticism of this item.
We have 525,000 of a vote to meet cases of that kind in the Maritime Provinces. I am quite aware that accidents will happen, but why should we make provision twice over?

I should like to get
through with this item if possible.
It will provoke considerable discussion.
Well, I have no objection to letting it stand. We have done a good day's work.

When we come to discuss this item I shall have something to ask about the Supreme Court Building. There was a talk of a new building, and I would like some information as to whether it is the intention to do anything in this respect. The present building is not worthy of the Supreme Court of Canada.

As far as I know, there is no provision for the construction of a new Supreme Court Building. I feel like 
agreeing with my hon. friend, but they seem to be getting on well as they are. There is a scheme on foot for the provision of new quarters for the Supreme Court when the next attempt is made at erecting public buildings in Ottawa. It will be across the street on the expropriated area. We are just preparing plans and models and getting ready for it, but it is not the intention to ask for an appropriation during the present year.

As a nation we are
proud of our public _buildings, but we are never very proud to show strangers the Supreme Court Building.

I quite agree with my
hon. friend.
It is the most important court in Canada and should have a building becoming its dignity.

While there is no item
providing for a new building I may say that if my hon. friend will go to the Public Works Department to the office of Mr. Ewart he will find material which will interest him. I think he would be pleased to go over the models of the buildings which are being designed for erection at some future date on Wellington street. One of the first, buildings he would come across in the plans and specifications and in the actual models is the new Supreme Court Building in conjunction with other buildings. It would be well worth the while of any member to spend two or three hours in Mr. Ewart's office looking over the models of buildings which it is hoped some day to erect on that portion of the Government property in Ottawa.
